- Published
Hundreds of thousands of people are without power after severe weather hit both coasts of the United States during the Thanksgiving holiday.
Eastern areas were lashed on Thursday by a powerful storm which broug
items.text:
Hundreds of thousands still without power after storms hit US on Thanksgiving
- Published
Hundreds of thousands of people are without power after severe weather hit both coasts of the United States during the Thanksgiving holiday.
Eastern areas were lashed on Thursday by a powerful storm which brought high winds, heavy rain and coastal flooding. Pennsylvania remained the state worst hit by power cuts early on Friday, according to monitoring site Poweroutage.us.
Conditions are forecast now to improve, though the National Weather Service (NWS) cautions that it will take some time. The West Coast has also been affected by its own storms.
Flight disruption also persists, with hundreds more delays and cancellations reported on Friday - which is expected to be another busy travel day.
More than 2,500 flights within, into or out of the US were delayed on Thursday, and more than 450 were cancelled, according to Flightaware.com.
One passenger told the BBC he had been stuck at New York's LaGuardia Airport for 13 hours while trying to fly to see friends in Chicago for Thanksgiving.
Beyond the travel disruption, impacts were widespread across the East Coast, and US President Donald Trump said he would consider releasing emergency funds.
Bridges closed in Maryland due to severe winds, while waves battered beaches in Delaware as water seeped onto the boardwalk.
On the wettest Thanksgiving on record in Washington DC, tidal waters surged and soaked runways at Reagan Washington National Airport.
The number of homes reporting power cuts peaked at close to a million on Thursday evening - with Pennsylvania, Virginia, Maryland and New Jersey badly affected.
Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro said utility providers were working tirelessly to restore power. In Maryland, almost two million customers were asked by authorities to limit their water consumption to essential use only due to "intermittent power disruptions".
Parts of eastern states are under states of emergency, including New York. Organisers of New York City's annual Macy's Thanksgiving parade have also postponed the iconic event to Saturday.
- Macy's postpones Thanksgiving parade due to severe weather 
  - Published1 day ago
On the West Coast, the concern was for exceptionally high tides and the associated risk of flooding.
Both San Diego and Los Angeles reported a high tide of over 8ft (2.4m) earlier this week, and beach-goers were advised to avoid coastal areas.
Train services along the Amtrak Pacific Surfliner, which runs along the California coastline, cancelled several trains due to "washout conditions from high tides", the company shared on social media.
Dramatic footage from Oregon showed a man and a dog being swept into the sea by a fierce, so-called king tide - but both escaped unharmed, police said.
In Miami, some travel delays persisted into Thursday after a FedEx plane overshot the runway the night before, which prompted the closure of all but one runway at the airport for a brief period.
A statement FedEx provided to US media confirmed that one of its flights had "experienced an issue upon landing". No injuries were reported, and the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is investigating what happened.
An airport employee who spoke anonymously to CBS News, the BBC's US partner, raised the possibility that rainy conditions had been a factor.
The American Automobile Association (AAA) predicted that 81.5 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles (80km) from home for the Thanksgiving holiday over a seven-day period.

items.title: Clashes mar European games as Macron condemns violence
items.summary:
Clashes mar European games as Macron condemns violence
- Published
Violent clashes marred a number of European football matches on Thursday night, with French president Emmanuel Macron condemning trouble at Marseille's home game against Levski Sofia.
There were also incidents at games between Turkis
items.text:
Clashes mar European games as Macron condemns violence
- Published
Violent clashes marred a number of European football matches on Thursday night, with French president Emmanuel Macron condemning trouble at Marseille's home game against Levski Sofia.
There were also incidents at games between Turkish side Besiktas and Israel's Hapoel Be'er-Sheva in Georgia and Sunderland's 1-1 home draw with Poland's Jagiellonia Bialystok.
In Marseille, the build-up to the Europa League match at the Stade Velodrome was affected by incidents in the stands, including the throwing of projectiles and flares between the two sets of supporters.
With 10 minutes to go until kick-off, several Marseille fans ran from a home stand, appearing to pursue a group of Levski Sofia supporters.
They breached the stand designated for away fans, which housed around 500 supporters of the Bulgarian domestic champions.
"Five people were taken to hospital with eye injuries, head trauma and a dislocated shoulder," said the Marseille police prefecture. "Six others were treated on site for various wounds."
Macron spoke to Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev about the incidents, with the French president condemning "with the utmost force these acts of violence, which have no place in sport or in public space", and reassured him that "these acts would not go unpunished".
According to news agency Reuters, Radev thanked Macron for his personal involvement following the "attack on Bulgarian citizens" and for the medical assistance provided to the victims.
Bulgarian President Iliana Iotova said she found video footage of the incidents "shocking" in a statement posted on social media.
"The attacks against the Bulgarian fans desecrate one of the great games that brings millions of people together around the world," she added.
"Everyone should be able to support their team without being afraid for their safety."
Ligue 1 club Marseille said it was "working to understand the precise circumstances of these incidents".
The police source said all the people injured were Bulgarian and there was "no information at this stage regarding any arrests".
Security personnel managed to restore calm, allowing the game to kick-off on time, although there were a few further flare-ups between the fans, notably during the half-time break in a match Marseille won 1-0.
"It's a very regrettable episode. These are incidents which are unacceptable for football," said Levski Sofia coach Julio Velazquez
Marseille boss Bruno Genesio added: "We are living through violent times in our society, so this is very, very regrettable."
Meanwhile, the Turkish Football Federation has strongly condemned the "unacceptable" actions of Georgian police towards Besiktas fans who unfurled a pro-Palestinian banner during their Europa League match against Israeli side Hapoel Be'er-Sheva.
Besiktas say they have lodged a complaint with European football's governing body Uefa over "disproportionate" use of force by Georgian police.
The match had been moved from Istanbul to Batumi, Georgia for safety and security reasons but had to be suspended in the 25th minute after clashes involving Besiktas supporters and local police.
Both the officiating team and the Besiktas players left the field, but play was able to resume 30 minutes later.
Besiktas won the match 2-1.
"We strongly condemn the unacceptable attitudes, behaviour and actions directed at Besiktas supporters inside and outside the stadium before and during the Uefa Europa League match," said a statement from the Turkish federation.
Turkish outlet NTV reported that Georgian police had gone into the stands and used pepper spray on the Besiktas fans.
The report added that there were anti-Israeli chants from the Turkish fans and that Besiktas players and director of football Onder Ozen spoke to supporters to try to calm matters before play restarted.
Hakan Fidan, Turkey's minister of foreign affairs, spoke to his Georgian counterpart Maka Botchorishvili following the incident.
"All necessary steps are being taken to ensure the safety of our citizens and protect their rights," a Turkish foreign ministry source said.
At Sunderland, there were crowd disturbances after Jagiellonia Bialystok fans were found in areas of the Stadium of Light with home fans, despite Uefa having imposed an away supporter ban for the Europa League game.
Police and stewards attended some disruption early on during the match.
"In the build-up to the match, the club had put measures in place in line with this sanction and maintained regular communication with our supporters, Jagiellonia Bialystok and Uefa," said a Sunderland statement.
"Unfortunately, Jagiellonia Bialystok failed to engage and cooperate on this matter.
"We are disappointed that these measures and communications were disregarded by some visiting supporters and we will review the circumstances surrounding their entry into the stadium."

Russia is in contact with US over diesel supply deal, deputy PM says
Russia's energy ministry is in contact with the United States regarding its deal to supply diesel, deputy prime minister Alexander Novak said.
Russia in ‌part lifted its diesel export ban after it struck a deal in October ‌with the White House as US President Donald Trump was seeking to bring down diesel prices ahead of the midterm elections. Despite this, no ‌Russian diesel cargoes have yet discharged in the US since the deal was made.
One diesel-carrying tanker, ‌the Agioi Fanendes, is drifting in the North Atlantic Ocean not far from New York according to LSEG data, after it briefly signalled for the port earlier this month. Novak had declined to comment on that tanker on Wednesday.
                                    
                        Russian sabotage incidents in Europe up 16 percent, UK-based defence think-tank alleges
Russian sabotage incidents on Europe rose 16 percent in the year to September 2026, with increasingly skilled operatives using more complex explosive methods, the UK-based International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) defence think-tank has said in a report.
Key allies of Ukraine have accused Moscow of waging a Europe-wide campaign of drone and cyber attacks ‌to disrupt their support for Kyiv, including an alleged attempt at a drone attack at Leipzig airport in August.
Moscow has rejected the accusations from Western governments and intelligence services.
The IISS ‌said that, while unskilled recruits still carried out most operations, a semi-skilled tier now used more complex methods, including improvised explosive devices with timed and remote detonators.
"Arrests remove proxies but are highly unlikely to deter the RIS (Russian intelligence services) that direct them," it ‌said.
The think-tank said Germany and Poland would remain the most targeted states, as their transport, logistics and industrial networks were key to supplying Ukraine.
                                    
                        Ukrainian drone attack on St. Petersburg wounds one woman
A woman was wounded and an apartment ‌building was ‌damaged in a drone attack on two districts ‌of Russia's ‌second-largest city of St Petersburg, local authorities said.
                                    
                        Unidentified drone briefly violates Latvian airspace
An unidentified drone briefly violated Latvian airspace in the early hours of Friday, the country's armed forces said in a statement.
NATO fighter jets ‌and an interceptor drone were deployed in response and an airspace violation alert for the eastern Ludza municipality was issued before being lifted shortly after, ‌the military said. A subsequent lower-threat alert for the Balvi municipality, north of Ludza, was also ‌reversed, it added.
The alerts were issued as Russia's Leningrad region was repelling a Ukrainian drone attack. The region’s Governor Alexander Drozdenko said more than 40 of the unmanned aircraft were downed.
                                    
                        Russia says drone attack wounded three people in port city of Novorossiysk 
A drone attack wounded three people in Russia's Black Sea ‌port city ‌of Novorossiysk after it hit three houses and a boiler ‌facility, Mayor Andrei ‌Kravchenko said on Telegram.
Novorossiysk is an oil and grain export hub and a major base for Russia's Black Sea Fleet.
                                    
                        Trump calls on Putin to halt 'military aggression' against Europe
US President Donald Trump said Thursday he had asked Vladimir Putin to "pull back all military aggression" against Europe.
Trump's comments come a day after he hosted NATO chief Mark Rutte in Florida, after which the two leaders issued a joint statement calling on Russia not to expand the Ukraine war.
"During my conversations in China with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, I spent a lot of time talking about the fact that I would like to see President Putin pull back all Military aggression against territories throughout Europe," Trump said on his Truth Social network.
Trump said he had done so "in the hopes that a Deal can be made between Russia and Ukraine, and made quickly".

items.summary:

The US FCC authorised the plan on Wednesday, calling it a first in the history of the country.

items.text:
Why does Elon Musk want to put a million satellite data centres in space?
The US FCC authorised the plan on Wednesday, calling it a first in the history of the country.
SpaceX founder and billionaire Elon Musk’s plan to launch a million satellites was approved this week by the United States, as controversy over data centres needed to drive the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution leads to a scramble for alternative locations.
On Wednesday, the US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) authorised the plan, named “Starmind”, and said it marks a first in the history of the country.
“At this pivotal time in America’s development of super intelligence [artificial intelligence], the FCC is granting SpaceX authorisation to deploy 1,000,000 orbital compute modules to process massive amounts of data to be used back here on Earth,” the FCC said in a statement posted on X by Chairman Brendan Carr.
Carr said under President Donald Trump’s leadership, the US was “moving decisively to ensure that this breakthrough technology creates opportunity, drives investment, and delivers benefits for the American people”.
“This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership and expand prosperity here at home,” he said.
Here’s everything we know about the plan to send a million satellites to space:
What is Musk’s plan?
With data centres being the crucial backbone behind AI computing, and with demand for the software rapidly growing, Musk’s plan provides an alternative: Using the sun as a power source for them.
According to SpaceX, which manufactures rockets and spacecraft, the new project works by using “satellites with localised AI compute, where the results are beamed back from [a] low-latency, sun-synchronous orbit”.
This, SpaceX claims, is “the fastest way to scale given the growing difficulty of finding electrical power sources on Earth”.
On its website, SpaceX calls the plan “low-cost [and] high performance”.
But Musk’s company already has satellites in space, with Starmind only expected to add to the constellation.
According to SatFleet Live, which tracks satellites in real time, there are 16,928 active satellites in orbit now. Of that, 11,190 (66 percent) are SpaceX Starlink satellites, the company’s internet outfit.
Under the FCC’s licence, SpaceX must begin its deployment of the satellite data centres no later than November 2033; send 10 percent of the maximum number, 100,000, no later than November 2035 in the same month; deploy 50 percent to space by November 2038 and the whole constellation by 2040.
Why does Musk want to send them up, and what’s the advantage?
As AI scales up rapidly, the need for data centres grows.
But data centres need vast tracts of land, and guzzle water and power, while churning out tonnes of fossil fuel emissions. They generate intense heat, and cooling systems need large amounts of water to keep the technology running, putting pressure on water supplies and communities facing drought, especially as climate change raises global temperatures.
According to an article published by the Environmental and Energy Study Institute, a US nonprofit, in 2025, “large data centers can consume up to 5 million gallons per day, equivalent to the water use of a town populated by 10,000 to 50,000 people.”
These concerns have set off mass protests against data centres, from the US to Kenya to India. Widespread opposition to data centres was a key issue for many voters in the US midterm elections earlier this month, per polling data.
In July, demonstrators against the rapid expansion of data centres held 142 protests across 42 states in a nationwide effort against AI infrastructure expansion.
Satellite-based data centres face no similar land constraints, and they can, in theory, use solar power – as SpaceX says is the plan – to fuel their processing. But cooling in space remains a challenge: Unlike on Earth, there is no air or water, so heat released can’t escape via conduction or convection.
Has there been pushback to the plan?
Yes.
Astronomers and environmentalists have criticised the plan, saying it will amplify sky pollution that makes it harder to see the night sky.
On Wednesday, the American Astronomical Society (AAS) said in a statement that it was “disheartened and dismayed” by the FCC’s approval of the plan.
“As the AAS stated in its earlier filings to the FCC, the proposed constellation would significantly undermine (i) decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities and (ii) the ability of astronomers and the public to enjoy and study the night sky,” the statement read.
“The AAS is gravely concerned about the future of federally funded astronomical research under such a fundamentally altered night sky, and the resulting waste of taxpayer dollars invested in astronomical facilities throughout the country and the world,” it said. “While we hope that SpaceX will continue to coordinate with the National Science Foundation, we remain concerned by the lack of formal coordination requirements in the license granted to SpaceX in this case.”

items.text:
‘I cannot go to work’: Iranians contend with pollution as well as US war
Hospital admissions for respiratory ailments have soared as the winter smog sets in.
Tehran, Iran – The headaches, shortness of breath and blurred vision which Ghoral, 40, a Tehran resident, once only experienced during the heavily polluted, cold seasons of the year have become year-round symptoms.
“The nausea hit me even before the Meteorological Organization announces that the air is polluted,” he tells Al Jazeera.
“On heavily polluted days, I try to leave the house as little as possible, which means I sometimes cannot go to work, affecting my income. At the same time, air pollution increases the cost of seeing a doctor and buying the medication I need to manage my breathing problems. All of this is happening simply because I have no choice but to live in a polluted city.”
The threat of American bombs is not the only danger the residents of Iran’s capital city must contend with these days: checking the air quality has become part of everyone’s daily routine.
Weather apps are no longer used primarily to check the forecast for rain or thunderstorms, but rather to view the latest readings on fine particulate matter (PM2.5) – the tiny, airborne particles which can be deadly when breathed in over a prolonged period.
Hossein, 36, a resident of the capital, tells Al Jazeera: “For someone like me, who both lives and works in the city centre, air pollution is no longer just a part of life; it has become life itself.”
There is little anyone can do about it except escape the city as often as possible, particularly during the winter months when pollution is at its worst.
“At the very least, I try to spend my weekends in nearby cities where the air quality is better,” Hossein says.
Remote work and traffic restrictions
The second half of the year in Iran has traditionally been a time of what is known as “temperature inversion”. This occurs when a layer of warm air traps cooler air and pollutants close to the ground, preventing them from dispersing.
While pollution has become a year-round problem, it is particularly bad in the winter, when this phenomenon is common, bringing prolonged periods of polluted air to cities and industrial areas.
Other major Iranian cities, including Mashhad, Isfahan, Shiraz, Tabriz and Ahvaz, are also grappling with air pollution.
For more than half of the autumn and winter months, air pollution warnings are regular, advising people with heart and respiratory conditions to take precautions. Children, older people and pregnant women are also advised to stay indoors and avoid outdoor activities.
In Iran, the Meteorological Organization uses a “yellow weather warning” to signal days on which air pollution levels are particularly high. On those days, schools typically cancel outdoor physical education classes.
When pollution levels approach the threshold for an “orange weather warning” – generally associated with an air quality index (on a scale of 0-500) above 140 – additional restrictions may follow. Some employees switch to remote work, traffic restrictions under the odd-even licence plate scheme are imposed to reduce the number of cars on the streets, schools are closed and some university classes move online.
Hospital admissions surge
Dr Hadi Yazdani, who works at a medical centre in Isfahan, tells Al Jazeera: “One of the first signs of rising air pollution is an increase in hospital visits by patients with chronic asthma and other respiratory conditions.”
According to figures from the Ministry of Health, hospital visits for these conditions, as well as for heart conditions, rise by as much as 50 percent in the winter. Eye and skin problems also tend to become more common as a result of air pollution.
“Children and older people are particularly vulnerable,” says Yazdani. “They may develop new illnesses or experience a worsening of existing conditions. In addition, because air pollution reduces the circulation of fresh air, respiratory infections such as influenza and COVID also become more prevalent.”
Evidence that hospitals across Iran experience a surge in emergency department visits as a result of air pollution has prompted the country’s Emergency Medical Services Organization to adopt different plans for managing patient demand during the colder months.
As pollution levels worsen, specially equipped buses are deployed in public squares in some of Iran’s major cities. They provide basic treatment for less severe pollution-related conditions, such as shortness of breath and chest pain. The buses are intended both to reduce the need for ambulances to travel across congested cities and to serve as the first point of contact for people seeking medical assistance.
This year, amid concerns that a renewed war with the United States could force schools to close again anyway, the Ministry of Education has also decided to delegate decisions about school closures due to air pollution to local education authorities.
Few remedies
Although air pollution in Iran is caused by both natural events, such as dust storms, as well as industrial and human-made sources, Iran’s Department of Environment has focused its efforts on tackling pollution caused by human activity.
Ahmad Taheri, head of the National Center for Air and Climate Change at the Department of Environment, tells Al Jazeera: “Alongside efforts to improve the standards of petrol and diesel used by vehicles, we are putting pressure on car manufacturers to produce vehicles that meet higher standards. We are also working to reduce gas flaring at refineries, which contributes both to air pollution and global warming.”
However, the efforts of Iran’s environmental authorities have done little to reassure the public about the country’s air pollution problem.

items.title: 'Massive for both' - Saints and Boro revisit Spygate rivalry
items.summary:
'Massive for both' - Saints and Boro revisit Spygate rivalry
- Published

The "noise" Southampton head coach Tonda Eckert refers to has been building over recent weeks, with 'Spygate' returning
items.text:
'Massive for both' - Saints and Boro revisit Spygate rivalry
- Published
"I don't want to shut out the noise, we just need to know that it's coming and it's going to be electric."
The "noise" Southampton head coach Tonda Eckert refers to has been building over recent weeks, with 'Spygate' returning to the collective consciousness as Saints and Middlesbrough meet on Friday (20:00 GMT) for the first time since the scandal.
The most recent time they came face-to-face was in last season's Championship play-off semi-finals.
Saints ended up winning over the two legs, but were then expelled from the final having being caught spying on a Boro training session before the first match at the Riverside.
It turned into a five-month saga which started with a Saints performance analyst being photographed from behind a tree, and ended with Eckert being handed a suspended ban and fined £28,000.
The German head coach signed a new deal at Saints exactly a week ago and previously admitted the experience of Spygate had changed his life.
Now St Mary's awaits as the two sides will re-ignite their rivalry after a tough end to the last campaign for both.
Saints players felt aggrieved for not being allowed to feature in the play-off final, while Boro suffered the heartbreak of losing at Wembley, as Hull City won promotion to the Premier League.
"It's a massive game for both teams," former Nottingham Forest and Ipswich defender Luke Chambers told the 72+ podcast.
"Middlesbrough have bounced back tremendously well from the play-offs, the ups and downs, they didn't know if they were coming or going, and to go through that heartache of making the final and not getting over the line - credit to them.
"It will be an electric atmosphere and there will be added needle on the pitch, especially with some of the things that happened in the games between the two sides last season when the news broke out."
- Hellberg reveals Eckert apology after Spygate 
  - Published8 October
- Southampton give head coach Eckert new deal 
  - Published6 days ago
- 'It's changed my life' - Eckert on Spygate scandal 
  - Published8 October
Hellberg and Eckert ready to move on - but can supporters?
Boro boss Kim Hellberg and Eckert both arrived at their respective clubs in November 2025 and have enjoyed plenty of success on the pitch over the past 12 months.
But following the 2-1 defeat in May's play-off semi-final second leg at St Mary's, Hellberg described it as "one of the toughest days" in his coaching career.
Although Friday's game promises to be filled with emotion on the pitch and in the stands, the two head coaches claim to have made up since the events of last season after Eckert called Hellberg to apologise over the summer.
"We spoke and he called me. I've always been a person who wants to give people a second chance," Hellberg told BBC Radio Tees.
"He has also gone though some things that have been very tough for him in terms of this which is something you don't wish anyone.
"I think in general for me it's overplayed. We have talked about it, everything has been sorted and now I'm looking forward to playing against a good side with a good manager and see how good we can be, and I'm really looking forward to it."
After Eckert took responsibility and apologised over the summer, both he and the club also expressed a desire to move on after the backing of the Saints board and owner Dragan Solak.
Some members of the Middlesbrough press have been robust and consistent in their strong criticism of Southampton and Eckert since Spygate first emerged.
Eckert had walked out of media conferences during the play-off semi-final following some stern questioning of him, while a piece was published on Thursday which questioned the German's character.
On Friday, Southampton published their own video, external on club channels, emotionally recalling the play-off campaign and how success was "ours... until it wasn't" before Boro "got another go", followed by footage of Oli McBurnie's winner for Hull at Wembley.
"People talk about last season, but we're focused on this one," narrates Southampton-based streamer Tyrone, over clips of goals from this season. "And now, here we are again; new hope, more reasons to believe, the same leader. We know all eyes are on us, and we're ready."
Southampton fan Rob Maddox echoed the emotions of both managers and felt that the majority of both fanbases want to now put the previous distaste behind them.
"There has been so much football since the play-off semi-final that I think both clubs are ready to get on with it now," he said.
"Some might look to hype the game up as a rivalry but I think the game should be looked at as two very good footballing sides going head to head.
"Of course there is going to be that little bit of spice and I'm sure we'll see it in the stands, but I hope that after the game we're talking about both teams showing off what they can do on the pitch."
Boro fan Jack McBride agreed that "Spygate's over and done with now" but admitted there was still a feeling of "bitterness" within the fanbases.
"I've seen some back and forth which is fun and all part of being a football fan, but there's also the other side of it which is bitter, twisted and they're still going on about it in a negative way," he told BBC Radio Tees.
"We had our chance and we didn't take it. Saints have had a four-point deduction, Tonda's been punished, we move on. Was it enough? Personally, I don't think that it was but we move on from it.
"This is a game we've all been looking to, and it was probably the first fixture that Boro and Saints fans were looking for.
"I think it's going to be quite a hostile atmosphere. I think Saints will be booing constantly and Boro fans will bring the noise as much as they can."

items.text:
Catholic Church: Victims of abuse may receive higher compensation
November 27, 2026
On Thursday, the Higher Regional Court of Cologne ruled that the Archdiocese of Cologne must pay €550,000 ($603,341) to a now 60-year-old woman. Melanie F.*, the claimant, was subjected to serious sexual abuse by a priest in the late 1970s and early 1980s.
This ruling could result in the Catholic Church paying significantly higher compensation to victims of abuse and sexual violence by priests.
The settlement far exceeds previous sums granted in similar cases. Before this, the highest financial compensation awarded by a court was €300,000. This amount was granted by the Regional Court of Cologne in June 2023 to a former altar boy who was abused by a priestfor several years.
Melanie F. was represented by the same lawyer. Since she had already received €360,000 in compensation during previous proceedings, the court granted Melanie F. an additional €190,000.
Abortion carried out without consent
In determining the appropriate amount of damages, the Seventh Civil Senate of the Higher Regional Court of Cologne pointed to an "abortion performed without the knowledge or consent of the plaintiff, who was only 15 years old at the time" as one of the deciding factors. The judges said that this incident in particular warranted a substantial increase in compensatory damages. The teenager reportedly became pregnant twice during the period of abuse.
Born in 1966, Melanie F. lived in a Catholic orphanage in Bonn in the late 1970s. Bernd U., then a theology student, worked there as a volunteer and cared for several children. After he was ordained as a priest, he took Melanie and a boy two years her senior from the orphanage to live with him.
Beginning in 1979, he subjected the underage Melanie to severe sexual abuse in his residence at the parish. He threatened to send her back to the orphanage if she refused to comply. He subsequently became the legal guardian of both children. Cardinal Joseph Höffner, who was then the Archbishop of Cologne, approved the arrangement.
In its written opinion, the court addressed the question of whether an archdiocese can be held liable for the criminal acts of a member of the clergy. The judges decided to overrule the Cologne Regional Court's ruling from 2023 and gave a detailed explanation of their reasoning. Ultimately, they found that the Church was liable under the principles of official liability.
The Regional Court had previously rejected this argument in 2023, siding with the lawyers of the Archdiocese of Cologne. At the time, the judges ruled that the abuse was not sufficiently linked to Bernd U.'s role as a priest. According to the judges, he had abused his foster child in his capacity as a caregiver, not as part of his priestly duties.
The 2023 ruling was met with disbelief and anger within the Archdiocese of Cologne. The archdiocese was already in turmoil because many Catholics were unhappy with how Cardinal Rainer Maria Woelki handled abuse cases. For decades, Church teachings and statements by Cologne's archbishops had repeatedly emphasized that a priest is a priest in all that he does and cannot simply set that role aside.
The Church's position served as a 'cover'
But now, the Higher Regional Court of Cologne has concluded that there is in fact a clear connection between Bernd U.'s work for the church and the crimes he committed. In their decision, they explained that he had assumed a pastoral role in caring for Melanie F. while she was still living in the orphanage and gained her trust through displays of great affection. His role at the church was described explicitly by the judges as a "cover." It was only much later that he sought to become the children's foster father, a position he would likely not have been able to obtain so easily without the "cover" of being a celibate Catholic priest. In addition, most of the abuse took place in the rectory.
After the ruling, Melanie F. said she was relieved that her years-long legal battle had finally come to an end. But she said she would never be able to put the abuse behind her. "You can't just block it out; you live with it."
The Archdiocese of Cologne said it "respectfully" took note of the decision.
The perpetrator, now 74 years old, was sentenced to 12 years in prison at his 2022 trial. The court found that he had abused nine girls, the youngest of whom was nine years old. The Church subsequently removed him from the priesthood.
"The strategy of the Archdiocese of Cologne to portray its priests' serious sexual crimes as the actions of private individuals has failed miserably," Thomas Schüller, a Catholic canon lawyer, told DW. Schüller described the archdiocese's approach as a "cynical attempt" that betrays the Catholic Church's own understanding of the priestly office.
From now on, the church will be held liable if a priest uses his position to sexually abuse children or teenagers and if the diocese or Protestant regional church has failed to fulfill its supervisory duties adequately.
'A day of hope for survivors of sexual abuse'
Schüller said that Germany's Catholic bishops must "significantly increase" compensation payments to survivors. Until now, the bishops had consistently argued that the amounts should be based on current court rulings and legal standards. However, this ruling will now have "significant financial consequences for both churches," he said. Schüller described the ruling as "a day of hope for many survivors of sexual abuse in both churches."
Matthias Katsch, spokesman for the survivor advocacy group "Eckiger Tisch," also called the ruling "good news." "Today, it was made clear that the Church must pay for the harm caused by its officials," he said. However, he added that the amount was still too low given the horrific nature of the crimes and their lifelong consequences. "The Archdiocese of Cologne's leadership turned a blind eye or acted with the grossest negligence," he said, allowing the crimes to hap

items.text:
Can luxury save Macy's?
Sign up for alerts on breaking news and exclusive reporting from NPR
Leaving the Macy's flagship store in New York, the Niesig family visiting from Germany sizes up their loot: a pair of sweatpants for mom, a Hurley jacket for dad, Ugg boots for their daughter. Son Mika, 16, is the only one empty-handed.
"I like zipper hoodies, and there was one zipper from Levi's that was pretty cool," he says. "But in the end, I didn't buy it because it was just a little boring."
As Macy's this week celebrates the 100th edition of its Thanksgiving Day Parade, the department store finds itself at a turning point. After years of questionable financial prospects, Macy's is trying to reinvent — as a luxury destination.
The retailer's gambit is to keep its old shoppers while also attracting new customers, who will perhaps pay more for real leather and upscale brands.
How Macy's got squeezed in the middle
Long before the pandemic, Macy's was grappling with America's shrinking middle class — and its own lack of fresh vision.
The department store business, to begin with, has become challenging. Big store space is expensive. Online competition is stiff. Shoppers are increasingly buying directly from their favorite brands.
And Macy's faces its own struggle. The chain is neither a discounter like Kohl's or T.J.Maxx, nor an upscale store like Bergdorf Goodman or Nordstrom. Macy's has languished in between.
"They were kind of like right in the middle," says Michael Prendergast, who advises retailers and brands at the consulting firm Alvarez & Marsal. "Now over time, that middle tier basically got crushed."
When the pandemic hit, store closures had Macy's forecasting an estimated $1.1 billion in losses. Its stock value dropped so low that the company was kicked off the big-league index, the S&P 500.
The way out is up
At one point, Macy's seemed to throw every other thing on discount just to get people buying something.
But it didn't work.
Stores looked disheveled and chaotic. Shoppers regularly noted a lack of workers to help on the floor. Over 2023, sales at Macy's dropped almost 7%.
Soaring inflation all but forced Macy's hand.
As the so-called K-shaped economy split the nation in recent years, folks with less money turned to Walmart or Target, which stepped up their game. Wealthier people continued to be the ones doing most of the spending, but also not at Macy's — leaning toward higher-end shops.
"For their size and scale the choice is almost made for them," says Prendergast, who's spent 20 years in the fashion business, including selling to Macy's at Tommy Hilfiger.
"If you're Macy's you say, 'We're still getting squeezed in the middle, our customer base in the U.S. is getting squeezed in the middle. Where can we go?' And really the only answer is to go up."
The new luxury vision
Luxury is now the big Macy's bet.
The retailer already owns the upscale Bloomingdale's, with its designer brands. Macy's also owns the luxury beauty chain Bluemercury.
In 2024, the head of Bloomingdale's took over the entire Macy's company and announced a turnaround plan, "A Bold New Chapter."
It included closing 150 stores and upgrading more than 300 others. Changes were proposed for the website and the staffing. Stores began to tackle clutter and add nicer items.
"We needed to remove the duplication, the redundancy," says Julie Walsh, senior vice president at Macy's whose team buys women's accessories and beauty products, including shoes, jewelry and makeup.
"When you come onto our floor now, it's a little bit lighter," she says. "So that the product that is on the floor shows up in a meaningful way."
Putting the higher prices to the test
In March, Macy's finally reported a year of growing sales.
The higher-end Bloomingdale's stores continued to drive much of the company's growth, but changes seemed to start paying off at Macy's, too.
Fancier options — like real leather instead of faux, brands like Ralph Lauren and Coach — have been raising the retailer's average selling price. It increased 9% in the latest quarter, executives said in September. They described shoppers' visits as "very steady and very significant."
Barb Anderson-Kerlin, a loyal Macy's shopper checking out the retailer's flagship in New York, says she's noticed a difference at the chain, after years of finding stores that seemed to ramble in all directions.
"The department store was like bedding, towels, pots and pans, perfume," she says. "Because I'd go in and just be overwhelmed. But now it feels like it's easier to see where the brands are."
How far can luxury sales take Macy's?
Still, most shoppers at the flagship store appeared dubious of the image of Macy's as a high-end chain.
"If they want to be luxury," says Chelsea Bates, who is visiting from Tennessee, "I would say serve champagne." She laughs, but notes that other upscale rivals do offer lounges and refreshments, like coffee.
Macy's insists it's not turning away from the middle class — just striving for more. Not picking a whole new lane, but widening the road in a gamble for this bifurcated economy.
"Macy's strength is being able to service our customer across all different categories in all different price points, and we're not changing that," says Walsh.
"What we are doing is making sure that we've got the elevated product," she says. "So it's not to replace it, it's an additive."
One hurdle is just how long Macy's had spent building its middle-price reputation, says Prendergast. Breaking out of the mold is a tough climb.
But, he says, if anyone can do it, maybe it is Macy's — having outlived many rivals over its 168 years.
"They're really the last man standing in that range for a reason," says Prendergast. "Everybody likes to count Macy's down and out, and they continue to prove everybody wrong."

items.title: Can Borussia Dortmund finally end their title wait? Three big questions for Bundesliga leaders
items.summary: Borussia Dortmund’s dreams have a habit of becoming nightmares, like when they somehow handed Bayern Munich the Bundesliga title on the final day of the 2022-23 season. Or when an 89th-minute Arjen Robben goal won the 2013 Champions League final for the same opponents. Whenever Dortmund suffer heart
items.text:
Borussia Dortmund’s dreams have a habit of becoming nightmares, like when they somehow handed Bayern Munich the Bundesliga title on the final day of the 2022-23 season. Or when an 89th-minute Arjen Robben goal won the 2013 Champions League final for the same opponents. Whenever Dortmund suffer heartbreak, it usually involves Bayern.
As things stand, however, Niko Kovac’s side hold a two-point lead over Bayern at the top of the Bundesliga. Both teams are unbeaten, but Dortmund may be the more stable of the two at the moment, especially with Harry Kane expected to miss several months through injury.
So can Dortmund make the most of this opportunity to become German champions for the first time since the Jürgen Klopp era? Or is another Dortmund dream destined to end in disappointment?
Will the data catch up with Dortmund?
The table never lies, apparently. The underlying data, however, can call into question the sustainability of a team’s position and, right now, it is casting serious doubt on Dortmund’s Bundesliga title prospects.
Dortmund rank a lowly 13th for expected goals (xG). Seven Bundesliga teams have scored more goals than the leaders, whose lack of open-play creativity is in stark contrast to that of Bayern’s – the Bavarians have scored 30 goals in 10 games and are still underperforming their own xG.
These attacking numbers haven’t been an issue for Dortmund given their defensive strength. Indeed, they are the most resolute defensive unit in the league, keeping more clean sheets than any other side. Having conceded only seven goals from an xG against of 13.4, though, there could be a correction coming.
The difference between Dortmund’s attacking and defensive stats is stark. While Ramy Bensebaini ranks in the top 10 for defensive contributions per 90 minutes this season, Dortmund do not have a single player in the top 30 for chances created. Fábio Silva is their most prolific shot-taker and he’s ranked 27th for shots per 90 minutes. This lack of statistical balance could be an issue over a full season.
Have Bayern’s injuries opened the door?
For Dortmund to win their first Bundesliga title in 15 years, they need Bayern to have an off season. That may be materialising such is the number of injuries the Bundesliga champions are having to handle right now.
Luis Díaz, Serge Gnabry and Manuel Neuer have all missed a large portion of the season while Ismael Saibari, Michael Olise and Alphonso Davies have also been absent through injury as Jamal Musiala continues to recover from a neurological condition. Most significant, though, is Kane’s absence. The Ballon d’Or winner, sidelined for a lengthy spell after undergoing surgery on torn ankle ligaments sustained in Bayern’s 1-1 draw with Cologne on Friday, has scored an incredible 156 goals in 163 appearances over the last four seasons and is Bayern’s creative heart. Without him, Vincent Kompany’s team simply do not pose the same threat, which was evident in this week’s Champions League loss to Lille.
Dortmund have injury troubles of their own. Giannis Konstantelias is out for the rest of the season after undergoing ACL surgery in September while Emre Can has not played since the spring. Compared to Bayern Munich’s crock list, though, there is not much for Kovac to worry about.
What can Dortmund learn from Leverkusen?
Bayer Leverkusen were the last team to disrupt Bayern Munich’s domestic dominance, winning the 2023-24 Bundesliga title under Xabi Alonso. Just like Dortmund, Leverkusen had a reputation for being perennial bridesmaids – indeed they were nicknamed “Neverkusen” for decades. That season, though, Alonso’s team demolished the rest of the competition, finishing a massive 17 points ahead of the chasing pack on the back of not losing a single game.
Leverkusen did not become nervous down the stretch because they were so far ahead from so early on. There is a lesson in that for Dortmund. They simply must capitalize on any Bayern Munich weakness while they can.
Under Alonso, Leverkusen were relentless. They played with intensity in every match and had an approach that reflected the ideals of their then up-and-coming manager. The BayArena was an exciting place to be and that came across in the energy of the team on the pitch. Dortmund have a different sort of energy, but Kovac has instilled a strong set of principles in his players and Dortmund’s form this season is a clear continuation of Kovac’s project. The Westfalenstadion faithful has ever reason to be hopeful once again.

Screen free tweens try their hand at Dungeons & Dragons

In its early days, some parents complained that the role-playing game kept kids holed up inside for hours at a time. NPR even did a 10 minute piece on it in 1979. In recent ye
items.text:
Screen free tweens try their hand at Dungeons & Dragons
Dungeons & Dragons has captivated players for more than fifty years.
In its early days, some parents complained that the role-playing game kept kids holed up inside for hours at a time. NPR even did a 10 minute piece on it in 1979. In recent years, D&D has come back into popular culture through shows like Stranger Things, a 2023 blockbuster movie and an influx of interest during the COVID-19 lockdowns.
Now, what was once a nerdy pastime has become a screen-free parent's dream – a game that relies on imagination, a role of the dice and in-person communication.
"It's a great concoction," Ted Fair says. He's the (grown-up) Dungeon Master for a group of nine to 12-year-old kids in Washington Heights in New York. "When you're able to sit down with … other people and harmonize like that."
Fair's group is part of Tweens Without Screens, a parent collective that focuses on providing technology-free activities for kids. They host things like knitting clubs and urban hikes. They have multiple D&D groups that meet monthly.
"I feel like part of what's kind of fun about it is we're trying to figure it out as we go along," said Rose Watson, a 12-year-old member of Fair's D&D crew.
In their most recent session, the group explored a cave and discovered a mysterious egg. Possibly a dragon egg? They didn't get a chance to find out! A low roll of the dice meant that instead of successfully stealing the egg, it crashed into pieces on the floor.
"It's like painting a picture in your mind," said Watson. She likes the in-person nature of the game. "A big part of it is getting together with other people and friendship and making jokes."
"And collaboration!" added her nine-year-old brother Leo Watson.
Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.
For fellow nine-year-old, Amos Slodounik, it's about getting to try on a different personality.
"You can express yourself in different ways. You can be goofy and nobody will care," he said.
And for Benjamin Cho, also nine, the fun is in the imagination. He spent much of the session drawing elaborate tools and creatures for their game (a healing spider donut, for example). "I like D&D because there's a lot of items and things that you can make up."
To listen to the full piece and follow along on the kids' D&D session, click above to listen.

items.title: Trump effectively ended asylum. Advocates look to the Supreme Court to restore it
items.summary:
Trump effectively ended asylum. Advocates look to the Supreme Court to restore it
For nearly two years, the Trump administration has prohibited asylum claims at the U.S.-Mexico border, canceled thousands of pending asylum applications and overhauled the immigration court system with mass firings. Cr
items.text:
Trump effectively ended asylum. Advocates look to the Supreme Court to restore it
For nearly two years, the Trump administration has prohibited asylum claims at the U.S.-Mexico border, canceled thousands of pending asylum applications and overhauled the immigration court system with mass firings. Critics say that combined, these moves have effectively shut down a once vital pathway for those fleeing persecution or danger.
The U.S. Supreme Court will soon consider whether the president can circumvent Congress and existing federal immigration law and unilaterally suspend access to asylum protections.
The legal challenge to the president's ban, which went into effect within hours of President Trump retaking office, is the latest legal case against the administration's seismic immigration policy changes that will be taken up by the high court. Those policy changes, critics say, have robbed asylum seekers of basic due process rights and have transformed the immigration court system into a deportation arm of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
In legal filings, the Trump administration has insisted the proclamation is a necessary protection against "invasion" along the southern border and what the president and conservative critics have long said is abuse of the system by "fake" asylum seekers. Since it has been in place, the chaotic crush of people crossing into the U.S. has plummeted. U.S. Border Patrol apprehensions dropped to their lowest level in agency history this year. The agency recorded fewer than 99,000 Southwest border apprehensions in fiscal year 2026 — a 95% decline compared with more than 1.8 million per year under President Biden, according to U.S. Customs and Border Protection data.
"The difference between an average month under Trump and an average month under Biden is just staggering," Simon Hankinson, a senior research fellow with the Border Security and Immigration Center at the Heritage Foundation, a conservative think tank closely aligned with Trump, told NPR. And should the Supreme Court reverse the ban, "it would be disastrous," he added.
Hankinson contends that most people arriving at the southern border don't qualify for asylum. "And even if they did, they've already passed through Mexico, which is a safe third country where they could claim asylum, especially if they're coming from Venezuela or Afghanistan. So you have a population that overwhelmingly will not qualify under U.S. law for asylum. They're here because they want to get a job," he said.
But, critics say, taken together the administration's moves have gutted access to asylum.
Despite newly restored quiet along the southern border, the president's argument for the asylum ban has been rejected by two lower federal courts. It has, however, remained largely in place as the case is tied up in court battles.
In December, the Supreme Court will review the administration's strategy of deporting immigrants to third countries that have agreed to adjudicate asylum claims, even as some of those countries face human rights abuse allegations and cannot guarantee that the person seeking asylum won't be returned to their home nation.
The administration faces a third legal battle that could end its attempt to indefinitely detain thousands of people in deportation proceedings.
If the majority-conservative court rules in favor of immigrant advocates in the lawsuits, advocates say, the decisions could finally break the choke hold that the Trump administration has had on asylum approvals, which are at their lowest in decades. National asylum denial rates soared to 94% in June, up from about 50% in 2024 — the last full year of the Biden administration. That's according to TRAC, a research project at Syracuse University that tracks data about immigration judges.
"The president does not have the right to unilaterally override the protections Congress has afforded those fleeing danger," said Lee Gelernt, lead counsel and deputy director of the Immigrants' Rights Project at the American Civil Liberties Union, one of the groups behind the challenge to the asylum ban. "The courts are right to reject this unprecedented power grab that would put countless lives in danger. We look forward to making our case before the Supreme Court."
Lawyers for migrants seeking asylum are hoping for wins at the high court. For several of Madhavi Narayanan's clients, this could be lifesaving. A Los Angeles-based immigration attorney with Human Rights First, she is currently representing immigrants who, prior to Trump's second term, would have had what she calls "slam dunk" asylum petitions.
One of them is a 30-something Ethiopian man called ZG, who arrived in the U.S. through Mexico in February 2025 after enduring extensive torture in his native country. Narayanan requested that NPR use only ZG because he fears retribution from the Ethiopian government. Upon turning himself in at the southern border, ZG was placed into detention and immediately filed an asylum petition.
Narayanan said ZG is a member of an Indigenous group in Ethiopia that's part of an ongoing armed conflict in that nation, which human rights organizations report is at risk of committing more atrocities against civilians. And, Narayanan, who has been working on the case for nine months, said she has produced documents and letters to support his claims of torture.
"Any other time, it would have been a really straightforward case," she said, adding that "there's a wide, wide range of human rights reports explaining that folks in this exact position would be at high risk" of violence and death if they were to return to Ethiopia.
But instead of an immigration hearing, ZG was given a deportation order this month to Uganda, a country he has never set foot in and one that does not recognize the military violence in Ethiopia as a war.

items.summary:
12 strategies to cut your risk of dementia. Take this quiz to start
Follow the Your Turn newsletter and listen to the Your Turn podcast on the NPR app or wherever you get your podcasts.
It's one of the biggest fears about getting older: losing your memory. A growing body of evidence shows we can do
items.text:
12 strategies to cut your risk of dementia. Take this quiz to start
Follow the Your Turn newsletter and listen to the Your Turn podcast on the NPR app or wherever you get your podcasts.
It's one of the biggest fears about getting older: losing your memory. A growing body of evidence shows we can do a lot to lower the risk of dementia, starting with changes to our day-to-day habits.
For decades, dementia was seen as something determined by genes or bad luck: a disease that strikes late in life with little anyone can do about it. That thinking has radically changed.
In 2024, the Lancet Commission, an international panel of experts, identified 14 modifiable risk factors for dementia and estimated that about 45% of dementia cases could be prevented or delayed. And lifestyle changes, when sustained over time, can be a powerful form of prevention. Last year, a large clinical trial from the Alzheimer's Association, called U.S. POINTER, found that older adults at risk of cognitive decline who combined physical activity, healthy eating, cognitive exercises and social activity could protect brain health, thinking and memory.
A score for your brain
So where do you start? One good place is a free, five-minute online tool called the Brain Care Score. You can take it with friends and family members as you gather for the holidays.
It was developed by Jonathan Rosand, a neurologist at Massachusetts General Hospital, and his colleagues. It's now supported through the Global Brain Care Coalition.
"The Brain Care Score tells you how to reduce your risk of brain diseases in the future, especially dementia, stroke and depression," Rosand says. "And it tells you what you can do to live a longer, more flourishing life."
The score covers 12 factors in three areas. The higher your score, the lower your risk. Those factors are:
- Physical health: blood pressure, blood sugar, cholesterol and body weight
- Lifestyle: diet, exercise, sleep, smoking and alcohol
- Social and emotional health: stress management, relationships and a sense of purpose
According to the coalition, the tool, "wasn't built to label risk. It was built to give people options and to show them that small changes made today can matter years from now."
Why blood pressure matters for your brain
High blood pressure might seem like a heart issue, but it's one of the biggest risk factors for dementia, and many people don't know their numbers.
"The higher your blood pressure, the more stress on your blood vessels," Rosand explains. "The more stress on your blood vessels, the more they break down over time," and the more they break down, the more likely they are to block or rupture. He says high blood pressure can increase the risk of stroke and dementia.
That's why the first step in calculating your score is to know your numbers: blood pressure, blood sugar (measured as A1c), cholesterol and body weight. You can ask your healthcare provider, check your patient portal or use a blood pressure cuff at a pharmacy. If you've been prescribed medication for high blood pressure, he says, taking the medicine is one of the most important things you can do.
Small gains add up
What if you take the quiz and don't love your number? The whole point of knowing your score is to use it as an assessment, a place to begin and a way to strategize about what changes you can make to your daily lifestyle habits. There's no need to overhaul your life.
In an analysis of real-world data from thousands of adults, each one-point improvement in the Brain Care Score was linked to up to a 4% lower risk of dementia, stroke or late-life depression. And even people who change their habits late in life can benefit.
The key is to pick one change that feels doable, such as:
- Adding 30 minutes of sleep to your daily routine if you're not well rested
- Putting an extra serving of greens on your plate
- Adding in a 20-minute walk each day and resistance bands for strength training
- Calling a friend to get together or joining a group activity
- Getting your blood pressure checked
Researchers say one healthy change often leads to others. Better sleep, for example, can make it easier to exercise and eat well, so the benefits can multiply across the score.
Purpose and connection count too
One part of the score that surprises people is the value placed on relationships and purpose. A 2025 study found that people with a higher sense of purpose were about 28% less likely to develop cognitive impairment.
That means joining the class or the volunteer gig you've been putting off can be considered a form of brain care.
You can retake the quiz over time to track your progress, and you can share it with family and friends. Healthy habits can be contagious.

It was a painful Sunday afternoon at Hull, but by the time Brighton pair Luka Vuskovic and Pascal Gross arrived at the beachside restaurant on Tuesday, you got the impression they didn't need too much of the bracing near-frozen sea air to boost the mood.
Yes, they were disappointed, but they weren't going to let a few minutes and Oli McBurnie overshadow a start to the season that has taken the Seagulls second in the Premier League table after 11 games.
Not many would have predicted such a lofty position for Fabian Hurzeler's team - including some of the Brighton team themselves - but the club are playing some thrilling football, and the 26 goals they have scored has helped them beat the likes of Arsenal and Man City already this season.

Sitting in front of me are two of the reasons why. They are both too modest to entertain that, but at the heart of this side's success is an almost seamless tactical and generational blend epitomised by Gross and Vuskovic.
Gross has been a revelation since his return earlier this year, something he admits he was nervous about doing. "You always hope for the best, but you never know. Coming back is not always easy."
The German international is making it look effortless. Opta have the 35-year-old top of their running stats, with 131.5km covered so far this league season, and only Declan Rice has more assists (4 vs 5).
But Gross' influence can't only be measured in numbers; this anchor or "connector" - as Hurzeler likes to call him - goes far beyond. No wonder his contract was recently extended for another season.
"I love the place, a lot of important things in my life happened here," he says.
"I have my family here, my kids are happy, my dog... it's a beautiful place with a lot of special people, where I feel really connected, really comfortable with the whole culture.
"We have so much talent and we have a lot of good people, but from different backgrounds. So that's really challenging, but I love the challenge because they're all good people we have in the dressing room.
"I was, at one point, a guy who came from another country, but I wanted to adapt, I wanted to be part of the culture. You need to help and support the guys. I really believe in what the club is doing. I think I can be a big part on and off the pitch."
The German international returned to Brighton after his dream move to Borussia Dortmund - the club he supported as a boy - ended early. He was desperate to show he could still perform at the highest level consistently. "I had to prove a point for myself, but also I wanted to repay the trust the club showed in me."
Do you remember playing better at any point in your career, I ask, telling him The Athletic had him as their number one player of the season so far.
"I don't believe in that. I don't see it like that. Maybe our start and the little things getting over-exaggerated.
"I think I am playing at my best, but maybe I think I'm a very good player in a good group who's working well, because everybody is improving. The way we set up, the way we play, I think everybody looks good."
Those stats, I say, are remarkable and again he down plays the praise. But he does concede: "They are really good, but because the team is playing well. If the team is playing well, everybody individually maybe looks a bit better."
Gross is honest enough to admit the start has surprised him. "No, I wouldn't say I expected that. I always hope for the best, but I know every game, like we saw on the weekend, is so different and so difficult that momentum can change quick."
Now, he says, comes the big challenge: the busy period. "It's a different sport, I always say". But you get the sense Brighton will be ready for it.
Alongside Gross, Vukovic has been another of the central characters in Brighton's success this season. He arrived in the summer from Tottenham in a club record deal worth £46m.
Vuskovic is no stranger to breaking records - two days after his 16th birthday, he became the youngest player to feature in Croatia's top flight. He is the fourth generation of his family to play football. Defending is very much the family business.
At 19, he has already played football in Croatia, Germany, Belgium and Poland, which has certainly helped him prepare for life as a central defender in the Premier League.
He says: "When you join as a 30-year-old guy, compared to say 15, instantly you have to grow up, you have to realise something in your life, and you have to mature.
"I had a really good group of people at Hajduk Split that made me mature fast enough, and they really helped me. In each of the countries, it was very helpful to develop, to grow as a human, as a football player."
Vuskovic's form in these first few months of the season has prompted a few questions about why Spurs let him leave in the summer and brought in Brighton's Paul van Hecke.
He doesn't see it as "rejection" and appreciates everything they did for him but, he adds: "In the end the coach came and said he didn't see me in his system, which is completely normal in football. I think in the end everybody earned (something). I gained experience, I moved to another club and I think we are all very happy about it.

items.title: The English Lamine Yamal? Why Williams-Barnett is getting Spurs fans excited

Why Tottenham's Luca Williams-Barnett earned Lamine Yamal comparisons from Roberto De Zerbi
Sky Sports' Callum Bishop takes a look into Tottenham's next big hope Luca Williams-Barnett after the teenager signed a new long-term deal at the club; watch Sunderland vs Tottenham live on Sky Sports Main Ev
items.text:
Why Tottenham's Luca Williams-Barnett earned Lamine Yamal comparisons from Roberto De Zerbi
Sky Sports' Callum Bishop takes a look into Tottenham's next big hope Luca Williams-Barnett after the teenager signed a new long-term deal at the club; watch Sunderland vs Tottenham live on Sky Sports Main Event on Super Sunday; kick-off 2.05pm
Wednesday 25 November 2026 14:13, UK
To earn comparisons to Lamine Yamal after just three Premier League appearances might seem a little far-fetched, but Roberto De Zerbi showed no hesitation.
So highly thought of is Luca Williams-Barnett at Tottenham that the remarks made following his stellar performance in the 2-0 win over Ipswich weren't all that shocking to hear.
"Luca is a special player. I'm not surprised because his talent is bigger than you think," De Zerbi said before simply saying, "yes, I think so," when asked if he could reach Lamine Yamal's level.

- Got Sky? Watch Premier League games LIVE on your phone📱
- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream PL games with no contract
The 18-year-old wouldn't even be halfway through his second year of A-levels, but his talent hasn't been a secret. The likes of Bayern Munich and Manchester United had already been linked with the starlet, so the news of a long-term contract at Spurs is one that brings unbridled joy among the fanbase.
An England U19 international, Williams-Barnett made plenty of headlines in his first start. Most notably, he became Tottenham's third-youngest Premier League goalscorer at 18 years and 51 days, only four days older than Gareth Bale, who is second on the list. That name certainly rings a bell.
The winger was also Spurs' sixth-youngest Premier League starter, and it's not just with his club that he's making history.
Just three other players have scored on their first Premier League start at a younger age, while he is only bettered by future Ballon d'Or winner Michael Owen as the youngest player to score and grab an assist in the same game.
The records are a great indicator of the talent that the youngster has. Famous Spurs wonderkids such as Harry Kane, Dele Alli and Glenn Hoddle had yet to make an impact at that age.
But what is it about his game that is really making people stand up and take notice?
De Zerbi said after the Ipswich victory that he asked Williams-Barnett "to play like he plays at the park with his friends, with the same freedom".
It's the sort of cliché that you often hear levelled at emerging talents. Where they often lack in experience and nuance, they make up for in fearlessness and often youthful abandon.
De Zerbi's request was never going to be a challenge for the teenager, though. That trait is what had already earned him admirers from those in the know.
"He deserves the opportunity to play. He's got the swagger, he's got the ability to play in that team," was Tim Sherwood's assessment before he had even kicked a ball this season.
While the swagger can't be denied, his trademark on the pitch is rather straightforward. Williams-Barnett's tendency is to slow the play down and keep the ball close to his feet before showing explosive acceleration to catch his marker off guard.
Though it isn't necessarily the most groundbreaking piece of skill, the youngster possesses an abundance of composure that sees him capable of going on the inside or outside. Something that Anan Khalaili found out the hard way during the youngster's cameo against Crystal Palace.
It's the sort of foundational skill that gave the likes of Ronaldinho and Neymar a platform to develop into the greatest flair players of their generation. Funny that Williams-Barnett should bear some resemblance considering the Brazilian duo appear to play a role in his pre-match routine.
"I've seen today in the bus from the training ground to the stadium, because he was very close with me, while we were coming in the stadium, he was watching on YouTube Ronaldinho, [Eden] Hazard, Neymar," De Zerbi disclosed after the Ipswich win.
He is clearly taking inspiration from what he has seen from these idols. If we are being critical of those superstars, the one thing the youngster might want to avoid adopting from them is their desire off the ball, as his head coach has already challenged him to.
"Work hard without the ball, like [Ousmane] Dembele, like Raphinha, like [Lamine] Yamal, because football is going in a different way and the first defenders are the attackers. Even if they are Ballon d'Or winners, or any players with talent, they have to work on the pitch."
To that degree, the gauntlet has been set by De Zerbi. But there is no doubting that Williams-Barnett has the backing of those at Spurs to go and make himself a huge success.
"What stands out most for me is his courage and bravery because as a young lad coming into Spurs first team and performing like that is not easy. He will have a very big future," said team-mate Omar Marmoush.
It has been over a decade since the club had a youth product that has captured the imagination in quite this way. Kane is the most obvious example, but not even he immediately made fans pay attention to this extent.
As is the case with every young player, patience is a virtue. But with a new contract, De Zerbi's blessing and a start to Premier League life that could hardly go any better, the sky is the limit for Williams-Barnett.
It is far too early to say exactly how far he goes. But if he shoots for the moon and misses, he will still become one of the stars.

items.title: Tarik Muharemovic: ‘Dad is at every Leeds game. I sometimes hear him shouting from the stands’

items.text:
Tarik Muharemovic is proving one of the best signings of this Premier League season and there will be special resonance when his upwardly mobile Leeds side host Coventry on Saturday.
Whereas Muharemovic’s father, Rasim, has been a matchday regular since the defender’s £34.1m move from Sassuolo, his mother, Elmedina, will watch her son play for Leeds for the first time.
The 6ft 4in Bosnia and Herzegovina centre-half credits his parents for a rise which has taken him to Wolfsberger in Austria and Juventus and Sassuolo in Italy before he joined Daniel Farke’s side in July. Rasim and Elmedina fled war in their homeland and moved to Slovenia, where Muharemovic and his brother, Kenan, were born.
“My whole story is down to my parents and everything I do is for them,” says the articulate 23-year-old, who speaks five languages and represented Bosnia at this year’s World Cup. “I think about them leaving their home, their family and friends and it was because of a war.
“Bosnia was in a bad situation; the whole of Yugoslavia was in a bad situation so they had to leave. They went to live in Slovenia for three years before moving to Austria because there were better jobs and more opportunities.
“My parents live there now but it’s still not easy when they look back at leaving their home and friends … yet they had to. They do everything for me and Kenan, who is at Rapid Vienna in Austria. He’s only 20 and some of my friends and family say he could be a bigger talent than me. He’s also a left-footed centre-back and we speak every day.”
During Muharemovic’s childhood, his father was relentless in helping him to realise his potential and not much has changed. “My dad would always be there asking: ‘Tarik, if you want to be the best, why didn’t you do this?’” Muharemovic says. “He pushed me to the limits, he was always there on the sidelines and still is now at every Leeds game. I can sometimes hear him shouting from the stands.”
Muharemovic quickly rose to prominence at Wolfsberger and after six first-team appearances he signed for Juventus aged 18 in 2021. He trained with the revered defenders Giorgio Chiellini and Leonardo Bonucci but a first-team appearance eluded Muharemovic and he joined Sassuolo, then in Serie B, initially on loan, in August 2024.
That proved the making of him as they were promoted as champions and Muharemovic thrived under Fabio Grosso’s guidance. He says: “Juventus was the best defensive school with a coach in Massimo Allegri who focused a lot on training and tactics and players like Chiellini and Bonucci.
“As a teenager, it was a privilege to train with these guys because they tell you everything you need to do. Chiellini would celebrate slide tackles and winning duels during games, so I like to do that too because my emotion comes out.
“I’ve always closely followed Virgil van Dijk’s defending and Edin Dzeko is a big idol of mine as a legend of Bosnian football. I’m very honoured and proud to have had such special moments with him, especially representing Bosnia together at the World Cup.”
Muharemovic’s World Cup experiences included a red card against Switzerland and being the victim of a challenge by Folarin Balogun which led to the USA forward being sent off, only for his one-game ban to be suspended by Fifa after an intervention by Donald Trump. The summer also brought interest from Inter and speculation about a return to Juventus before Leeds signed him on a five-year deal.
“I had a few teams interested in me but the dream has always been to play in the Premier League,” says Muharemovic, who captained Bosnia for the first time against Romania this month. “I had an amazing call with the boss [Farke] about the project at Leeds and just had to say yes. He’s built a family here and there’s a huge togetherness with all the players, staff and fans.”
Leeds thumped Chelsea 4-1 last weekend in their first win at Stamford Bridge since 1999, prompting talk of a push for European qualification. They have not conceded in the opening 22 minutes in the past 43 matches and belief is growing.
“We all dream about Europe and playing on the big stage,” says Muharemovic, whose performances for Leeds have attracted admiring glances across the continent. “It would be very deserved and special if we can do it for us as players, the fans and the club … I’m just happy with what I’m doing for me and my family and to show those people who didn’t believe in me that I can do it.
“Everyone knows the Premier League is the most difficult league in football but I never doubted myself. I know my qualities and I’m having a good season but it’s very early so I just need to keep playing consistently.”
Looking ahead to his parents’ visit, Muharemovic, a Muslim who prays five times a day, says: “It’ll be very emotional when I see them together at Elland Road for the first time. My dad has been to every game so far and was in the away end in the opening match at Nottingham Forest. I thought the families would sit in a different part of the ground, so when I saw him sat with the Leeds supporters as I was warming up, I was like: ‘Oh my God, good luck!’
“I know what Leeds fans are like so I was thinking: ‘I just hope no one jumps over him,’ but he absolutely loves it. Now my mum is coming too, it’s special and I can’t wait so hopefully we can celebrate with another win. Yes, I’m living the dream but I’m just getting started and always want to show more and achieve more.”
