Why is India so afraid of Pakistan's new Netflix series?
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on:
PRESS REVIEW – Friday, November 27: Controversy brews as India asks Netflix to ban a Pakistani series from being broadcast in the country. Tensions have been high between the two nations since last year's terror attack in the Kashmir region. Also in the news: Taiwanese voters will head to the polls for all-important local elections overshadowed by the threat of Chinese claims to the island. Finally, forget schadenfreude – practicing "freudenfreude" is better for your health.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government has asked Netflix not to air a Pakistani series in India. The story is getting front-page coverage in the Indian press. The Asian Age and The Hindu report that Netflix's first-ever local Pakistani production will be released next month. "Jo Bachay Hain Sang Samait Lo" is a cross-generational romance starring prominent Pakistan actors. But Indian cinema federations want the series banned from broadcast in India. The Hindu explains that two groups, the All Indian Cine Workers Association and the Federation of Western Indian Cine Employees, have called for a ban on Pakistani content. It comes after last year's terror attack in the state of Jammu and Kashmir, in which 25 Indians were killed.
The Indian Ministry of Information and Broadcasting has now asked Netflix to ban the series from being broadcast, a request to which the streaming giant has not yet responded. The Hindu explores the "legal basis" for India's demands – noting that it stems from a constitutional article pertaining to broadcasting content that threatens the "unity, defence, security, integrity or sovereignty of India". A writer for the Asia Times slams India's reaction, asking: "Why is India so afraid of Pakistan's Netflix love story?" The writer reminds us that culture is important because it "creates spaces in which societies recognise one another beyond the boundaries of official narratives". The article compares India's reaction to George Orwell's "1984" – saying it says more about India's confidence in its own cultural industry than anything else. India's reaction is "ironic given that Bollywood itself has benefited from the ability of film and TV to cross political, linguistic and geographical boundaries", it says. The Balochistan Pulse, an online Pakistani news website, suggests that India feels threatened by the popularity of Pakistani dramas – citing this as a plausible reason for the move to ban the series in India.
Staying in Asia, the people of Taiwan will head to the voting booths this weekend in closely watched local elections. Voters will choose mayors, council members and local leaders in 22 districts on Saturday. Key electoral issues will include housing affordability and wealth distribution. This comes, however, as the spectre of China looms large, with tensions over China's increasingly vocal sovereignty claims over Taiwan.
The Taipei Times reports that Premier Cho Jung-tai has raised the alarm over cyberattacks. The Taipei Times says China has been targeting Taiwan's systems constantly, with an average of 2.58 million intrusion attempts per day. The editors of the Taipei Times say the elections are "a bellwether and a litmus test" for President William Lai and the ruling DPP party, which lost badly in local elections five years ago. It will also be an assessment of the leadership of the main opposition KMT party – and its chairwoman Cheng Li-wun – whose China-leaning policies have been widely questioned. Editors urge voters to show "the nation's democratic resilience and their determination to safeguard Taiwan's sovereignty."
The Washington Post explains that China is targeting the Meta app "Threads" in Taiwan. The short messaging app is hugely popular on the island and accounts for 10 percent of all Threats website traffic. Users share everything from fortune telling to dating to lost-and-found notices, the Post says. They also discuss political and social movements, plus the weather. Officials say they have found China-linked accounts on Threads that are trying to sway voters. Taiwan has flagged some 2,400 accounts to Meta.
Finally, we have all heard of schadenfreude, but The Washington Post says it is time to practice "freudenfreude"! Schadenfreude is the German word for taking pleasure in someone's misfortune. "Freudenfreude" is the opposite – taking joy in someone else's joy. According to the paper, a small US study in 2022 assigned people with symptoms of anxiety and depression to partake in three activities: social connection, behavioural therapy or acts of kindness. All three activities improved their lives – but acts of kindness seemed to have the biggest effect. The key is to be sincere – when something good happens to a loved one or a friend, be there for them and enjoy their success and you will feel better too.

items.summary:
Democrats want to end Trump’s Iran war. But how different are they?
Decades of bipartisan pressure on Tehran raise questions about how far they are willing to change US policy.
The Democrats’ thumping victory in the United States midterm elections this month came amid widespread public opposition to
items.text:
Democrats want to end Trump’s Iran war. But how different are they?
Decades of bipartisan pressure on Tehran raise questions about how far they are willing to change US policy.
The Democrats’ thumping victory in the United States midterm elections this month came amid widespread public opposition to the US-Israel war on Iran, which has sent energy prices soaring across the country and globally.
Democratic Party leaders, including those regarded as traditionally more hawkish on Iran, have called for an immediate end to the nine-month war.
“We have to work and move aggressively to end the reckless and costly war of choice in Iran right out of the gate,” presumptive incoming House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries said last week, when asked about his priorities come January.
A day after the Democrats’ decisive victory, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, who opposed the landmark 2015 nuclear agreement with Iran, said Americans did not know “what the heck we’re fighting for in Iran”.
But the Democrats’ electoral triumph has been met with scepticism in Tehran. Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has warned that anyone expecting the election outcome to change Washington’s policy towards Iran is “seriously mistaken”.
While Democratic opposition to the war has drawn a distinction between the party and Trump, analysts are sceptical about whether it reflects a fundamentally different approach towards Iran – a country that successive US administrations, Democrat and Republican, have sought to isolate diplomatically and economically.
Decades of bipartisan hostility
For much of the period since the 1979 Islamic revolution, hostility towards Iran has superseded partisanship in Washington.
It was under Democratic President Jimmy Carter that the US began imposing sanctions on Iran following the seizure of the US embassy in Tehran, eight months after US-backed monarch Mohammad Reza Shah Pahlavi was overthrown in a popular uprising led by former Supreme Leader Ruhollah Khomeini.
Successive Republican administrations maintained pressure on Iran. But it was Democratic President Bill Clinton who substantially expanded its economic isolation through a policy of “dual containment”, targeting both Tehran and Iraq under its former president, the late Saddam Hussein.
In 1996, Clinton signed legislation imposing sanctions on foreign companies investing in Iran’s energy sector, a move that enjoyed overwhelming bipartisan support, with the bill passing 415–0 in the US House of Representatives.
Even when Washington and Tehran found common strategic interests, opportunities for rapprochement were short-lived.
Following the September 11, 2001, attacks, Iran cooperated with the US against its common foe – the Taliban in Afghanistan — helping end their first stint in power. Yet, just months later, Republican President George W Bush branded Iran part of an “axis of evil”, alongside Iraq and North Korea.
“Bush’s proclamation shocked both reformists in Tehran and those US military leaders who were collaborating with the Islamic Republic at the time,” Golnar Nikpour, a historian at Dartmouth College, told Al Jazeera.
For Maryam Jamshidi, associate professor of law at the University of Colorado Boulder, such hostility is rooted partly in Washington’s unwillingness to accept Iran’s independent regional influence — a legacy of the 1979 embassy takeover and Israel’s influence on US foreign policy.
“When it comes to Iran policy, there hasn’t been much variation between Republicans and Democrats,” Jamshidi told Al Jazeera. “Both parties have broadly viewed post-revolutionary Iran as an enemy to be constrained, marginalised, and suffocated.”
“Indeed, until Trump, the worst rounds of Iran sanctions came under Democratic presidencies, specifically Clinton and Obama,” she said.
In 2010, Obama intensified economic pressure on Tehran by signing into law the Comprehensive Iran Sanctions, Accountability and Divestment Act, targeting foreign companies supplying Iran with refined petroleum products or helping expand its oil refining capabilities. The bill passed by an overwhelming majority of 408-8 in the House and 99-0 in the Senate.
But according to political analyst Negar Mortazavi, the continuity of economic pressure does not necessarily mean the two parties have pursued identical policies.
“It would be historically inaccurate to suggest that their approaches towards Iran have been essentially the same,” Mortazavi, senior non-resident fellow at the Center for International Policy, told Al Jazeera.
The distinction, Mortazavi argued, is particularly evident in the contrast between Obama’s “diplomatic breakthrough” and Trump’s decision to wage war.
Obama’s pivot and Biden’s retreat
While the Obama administration helped impose sweeping international sanctions on Iran, it also challenged decades of US foreign policy by engaging directly with Tehran, culminating in the 2015 nuclear agreement.
Under the agreement signed in Vienna with six world powers and the European Union, Iran agreed to curb its uranium enrichment activities and pledged not to develop nuclear weapons. In return, the US loosened many of the sanctions against Iran and released some of Iran’s previously frozen funds.
“The JCPOA was much more than a nuclear agreement,” Mortazavi said, referring to the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action. “It represented the possibility of a fundamentally different relationship between Washington and Tehran, based on diplomacy rather than confrontation.”
During Obama’s second term, the US and Iran also tacitly cooperated in fighting a shared enemy in ISIL (ISIS), especially in Iraq.
However, that did not mean Obama’s diplomatic outreach to Iran was without pushback within his own party.
Among the Democrats who opposed the nuclear agreement was the staunchly pro-Israel Schumer, now one of the most prominent voices calling for an end to Trump’s war.

items.text:
Five people hospitalised as Levski Sofia and Marseille fans clash ahead of Europa League game
Fighting broke out ahead of Thursday's Europa League match between Levski Sofia and Olympique Marseille, with five Bulgarian fans ending up in hospital. Local media reported a number of Levski fans performing Nazi salutes in the lead-up to the skirmish.
Five Levski Sofia supporters were taken to hospital after violence ahead of the Europa League game at Marseille on Thursday, with the French and Bulgarian presidents blaming the home fans.
The lead-up to the match at the Stade Vélodrome was marred by confrontations in the stands between the two sets of fans, including the throwing of projectiles and flares.
Footage widely shared on social media showed a Levski supporter performing a Nazi salute in the direction of the Marseille fans before the violence broke out. Local media reports alleged the gesture was repeated by multiple Bulgarian fans in the lead-up to the skirmish.
Watch moreLyon held and Marseille pushed in mixed Europa League night for French clubs
French President Emmanuel Macron condemned "in the strongest possible terms ... acts of violence targeting Bulgarian fans", the Élysée Palace said.
Bulgarian President Iliana Iotova called it "unacceptable" and "shocking".
"The attacks against the Bulgarian fans desecrate one of the great games that brings millions of people together around the world," she said in a statement on Facebook.
"Everyone should be able to support their team without being afraid for their safety."
Macron spoke to his Bulgarian counterpart on the sidelines of a European summit in Brussels, assuring her that "these acts would not go unpunished", the Élysée said.
Several hundred Marseille fans ran from the stand where they were situated about 10 minutes before kick-off, appearing to pursue a group of Levski supporters.
They breached the stand designated for away fans, where around 500 visiting fans were gathered.
Fighting broke out, with several Marseille fans wearing face coverings, an AFP journalist at the scene said.
'Violent times'
"Five people were taken to hospital with eye injuries, head trauma and a dislocated shoulder," a source with the Marseille police prefecture told AFP.
"Six others were treated on site for various wounds."
The police source said all the people injured were Bulgarian and there was "no information at this stage regarding any arrests".
Manuel Bompard, an MP for the left-wing France Unbowed (LFI) party for Marseille's Bouches-du-Rhône department, commented on a video shared online showing a Levski fan performing a Nazi salute.
"The far right has no place in our stadiums!" he wrote on X.
Iotova called on French authorities to "clarify the circumstances surrounding the attacks and look for responsibility from those who committed them".
She urged European football's governing body UEFA to "check how the safety of the Bulgarian fans at the stadium was ensured".
"We are ready to provide the necessary assistance to our compatriots. This behaviour is unacceptable!" she said.
Security personnel eventually managed to restore calm as the game kicked off on time.
There was another flare-up between opposing fans during half-time, before the match ended 1-0 to the hosts.
"It's a very regrettable episode – these are incidents which are unacceptable for football," said Levski coach Julio Velazquez.
"I support the fans who were caught up in this incident. I hope nothing serious has happened. I'm very saddened by this situation."
Ligue 1 club Marseille said it was "working to understand the precise circumstances of these incidents".
"We are living through violent times in our society, so this is very, very regrettable," said Marseille coach Bruno Génésio.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

items.title: Zelensky criticises 'strange' Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview
items.summary:
Zelensky criticises 'strange' Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview
- Published
Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, criticising Donald Trump for calling Vladimir Putin "my friend" and saying delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles were costing Ukrainian lives.
In
items.text:
Zelensky criticises 'strange' Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview
- Published
Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, criticising Donald Trump for calling Vladimir Putin "my friend" and saying delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles were costing Ukrainian lives.
In an interview with the BBC at his central Kyiv office, Ukraine's president complained the US was not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks, and called it "strange" that Trump posted a photo of himself embracing Putin.
"Of course it's up to the President of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English.
"He's an aggressor, and a killer…He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, adding it was like saying you were friends with Adolf Hitler during World War Two.
Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the United States.
Trump's two envoys have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.
The latest round of peace talks, mediated in Abu Dhabi earlier this month, made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.
He said talks were expected to resume in December.
On Thursday, Donald Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that at his own summit with Putin in China last week he had urged Russia to "pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe" and said he believed a peace deal with Ukraine was "a strong possibility".
But from its public statements, Russia appears to have regressed to its initial, hardline negotiating positions – on everything.
And Zelensky revealed that it was not clear whether European negotiators would be at the table, as the US envoys had announced.
The Kremlin appears to be resisting.
- Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say 
  - Published7 days ago
- Zelensky says Putin is a 'killer' after Trump calls Russian leader a friend 
  - Published6 days ago
Ukraine urgently needs the talks to move forward and bring five exhausting years of Russia's full-scale invasion to an end.
Russian strikes across the country have been growing more frequent and more deadly: the number of civilians being killed is at an all-time high.
So Zelensky called for "real helpful allies, who can push Russia" to achieve results and urged the US to live up to its reputation as a strong country with "power and respect".
"When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor... it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It's not right," he said.
The US argues that it is neutral: in the complex search for a peace deal between the two sides that can hold.
Questioned again on Thursday about calling Putin a friend, Trump told reporters: "We want to stop killing. I could say he's not a friend... I want to make a deal."
He added: "I could walk in and say, I don't like you, and then we have the same problem that we have with Zelensky and Putin.
"You know... the biggest problem to that settlement is the fact that you have two leaders that really hate each other."
In the meantime, Kyiv is struggling to defend its skies.
The air alerts, day and night, are now a draining feature of everyday life. As Russian ballistic missiles target power stations and bridges, jet-powered drones are launched daily at central Kyiv and other big cities.
Ukraine launches hundreds of drones at targets in Russia in response.
Zelensky said the military here are now able to destroy about 70% of Russia's fastest drones, a statistic he said was improving.
But there is a "very, very big" deficit of interceptors to stop ballistic missiles and he said the Americans were delaying deliveries of its Patriot systems.
"It's a pity they made a focus on Middle East and they help them more… It's a pity. We have huge questions with this," Zelensky said.
"The deficit of these missiles - that is people's lives."
He also confirmed that the US satellite communications system, Starlink – and its military version, Starshield – were still being restricted in occupied areas of Ukraine.
Ukrainian drone units have described their problems to the BBC, as their interceptor drones can no longer catch up with Russian Shaheds. It means those weapons then fly deeper into Ukraine, unhindered.
So whose decision was that?
"Technically SpaceX, politically - I don't know, I really don't know," Zelensky replied. "It's like... ping pong. We are asking one side, they say it's the other."
Tough winter
Ukraine's own long-range strikes against Russian targets have increased in recent weeks, including oil refineries and ships carrying weapons or fuel.
On Thursday, Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said an attack that sank a Russian warship docked in eastern Libya this week risked spreading war to the Mediterranean, which was unacceptable.
Zelensky defended the move, calling the warship Merkury an "absolutely fair goal".
He accepted that such strikes were "very dangerous" but said Ukraine's forces "never attack" without co-ordinating with its partners.
He declined to be more specific.
But he acknowledged that Ukraine was bracing for a difficult and dangerous winter.
Recent attacks on Kyiv have targeted bridges over the vast river Dnipro, apparently trying to cut the city in two.
Some residents have already left town for the winter and businesses closed, as power cuts and strikes on logistics networks have pushed operating costs unmanageably high.
They have also plunged much of the city into darkness.
"[Russia] wants us to run away, of course," Zelensky said.
"People can go, but we will try to defend our capital in any way. We need our capital. Without a capital, you don't have a country."

The six fishermen crossed the maritime bo
items.text:
South Korea sends rescued fishermen back to North
Pyongyang has not commented on a seventh fisherman who chose to remain in the South.
South Korea has repatriated six of the seven North Korean fishermen it rescued from their drifting boat earlier this month.
The six fishermen crossed the maritime border between the rival states off the Korean Peninsula’s east coast on board their vessel early on Friday. They were met by a waiting North Korean ship.
On November 3, the South Korean military and coastguard authorities had rescued and towed the fishing boat after it drifted into international waters near the country’s Ulleung island.
South Korea has confirmed that the six men sent to the North had expressed a wish to return. A seventh fisherman chose to defect, according to the Unification Ministry.
Seoul added that it had notified Pyongyang of the plan through the multilateral United Nations Command, and also sent updates on Friday over an international maritime communications network.
North Korea has not commented on the fisherman who chose to remain, but the waiting vessel suggested that Pyongyang had received all communications.
North Korea severed direct communications with the South in 2024. Border tensions have escalated between the two this year.
South Korea considers North Koreans as its citizens and offers protection to defectors or repatriates those who wish to return.
Pyongyang usually takes defections seriously and has accused the South of enticing its citizens to the other side, a charge that Seoul denies.
Some 31,500 North Koreans were registered as living in the South by June, according to Unification Ministry data.

items.title: 'Man Utd being relegated would be the biggest shock in history... but it won't happen'
items.summary:
Man Utd being relegated would be the biggest shock in history, but it won't happen, says Paul Merson
Manchester United take on Brentford on Saturday with Mauricio Pochettino looking for his first win to take them out of the relegation zone; Arsenal then take on Man City, live on Sky Sports this Sund
items.text:
Man Utd being relegated would be the biggest shock in history, but it won't happen, says Paul Merson
Manchester United take on Brentford on Saturday with Mauricio Pochettino looking for his first win to take them out of the relegation zone; Arsenal then take on Man City, live on Sky Sports this Sunday, the reigning champions are aiming to go nine points clear of Enzo Maresca's side
Friday 27 November 2026 09:20, UK
In his latest Sky Sports column, Paul Merson previews a big weekend for Manchester United, before Arsenal take on Manchester City in a huge game live this Sunday.
Mauricio Pochettino is looking for his first win as United boss as he bids to take them out of the relegation zone. However, Brentford visit Old Trafford on the back of their recent win over Everton, which took them into the top six.
- Premier League Predictor - play our new game
- Got Sky? Watch Premier League games LIVE on your phone📱
- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream PL games with no contract📺
Then on Sunday, Arsenal host title rivals Man City. Enzo Maresca's side are already six points behind the reigning champions and have won just two out of their last seven matches in all competitions.
Read below for the Magic Man's thoughts ahead of a huge weekend in the Premier League...
'Brentford game is massive for Man Utd'
Manchester United are in trouble. 100 per cent. Of course they are. But I don't see them getting relegated, absolutely not.
I would be shocked and amazed, it would be the biggest shock in the history of anything. People will go: Mike Tyson got beat by Buster Douglas. But that was one punch. This is over 38 games.
Brentford is a massive football match for them. If they lost that game, I don't see them beating Newcastle if Matthias Jaissle's side get anywhere near the level they played against Arsenal in the second half.
Then by the time you're playing Coventry, you're more than a win away from getting out of trouble. As soon as that starts happening, that's when it starts getting worrying - when you need two weeks to get out of the bottom three, or four or five points away.
The next three weeks are massive for United. If they beat Brentford this week, that will settle them down.
But I look at the teams down there right now. Crystal Palace won't go to Old Trafford and win. Sunderland and Nottingham Forest won't. Fulham and Coventry won't. Hull won't. So that means to me that Man Utd are better than them.
That's why I don't see them getting relegated. When you look at it like that, there are a lot of worse teams than them.
Man Utd have bought too many 'four or nines' - that's what I call them. They're either 4/10 or 9/10. They're not in between. You can't do that at Man Utd. You have to be between a seven or an eight on a consistent basis. You can't be four one week and nine the next, it doesn't work.
The pace of the game is controlled by the other team, it's never controlled by Manchester United.
They have got no defenders. They've gone it horribly wrong, trying to build from front to back. But it's more than that, it's spine of the team.
They need a centre forward. They don't have a dictating midfield player who comes short and controls the game. The only way United can do that is if they sacrifice Fernandes going forward and playing him deeper, like a quarterback - and then hope you've got enough going forwards elsewhere.
I don't see anyone else in that United team who is capable of coming deep and playing the ball forward. Playing that pass on a consistent basis, making the right decisions.
'Man City have lost their fear factor'
Man City have got to go out and play for the fans, they're the ones who are paying their money. They're getting paid £300,000-a-week, the fans are the ones paying to watch them.
Man City are getting a little bit found out. I have always said, even when they were playing at their best, they give you chances. And you have to make those chances count.
It used to be: go to the Etihad, get your stomach's tickled, get out with a 3-0 defeat that you're more than happy with that, and go back on the coach - because they could win games by six or seven.
Then all of a sudden, they started winning games but they were also open at the same time. And now, teams don't fear them.
Teams know they will get chances if they have a go at them - and enough chances to win football matches, not just one or two chances.
If you are brave enough - like Fulham were by getting players in the opposition box - you can beat Man City.
This is the problem for them: they're too open and there's not that fear factor anymore. And I also don't think Erling Haaland gets the service he deserves.
You would like to think that City's players aren't being affected by the charges hanging over them, because no one knows what is going to happen. So you have to play until you know what's going to happen.
It's like life: no one's going to tell you what's going to happen tomorrow, so live today.
'If Arsenal beat Man City, the league could be over soon'
If Arsenal win this game, the league is finished. That would be nine points clear and this league could be over very, very quickly.
Arsenal were dominant in the first half against Newcastle and if it was a boxing match, then Newcastle would have thrown the towel in.
They came out the second half a bit lackadaisical and Newcastle were outstanding by playing on the front foot. But then Arsenal switched and decided they weren't going to lose.
And then they scored one of the best goals of the season. If the finish from Noni Madueke was good, it would be the goal of the season. But when you see the finish, it's not great and the goalkeeper should save it. If he whips it into the far corner, it's goal of the season.
I think we saw enough with Brighton last weekend against Hull. That's one of those games where you go: if you can't win it, don't lose it.
You feel sorry for Brighton, because Konstantinos Tzolakis was unreal. He should be playing for the New York Rangers t

Transitional President Gen Horta N'Tam announced in a decree that the presidentia
items.text:
Guinea-Bissau's military leaders delay return to civilian rule until 2028
- Published
Guinea-Bissau's military rulers have postponed elections scheduled for next week by two years, delaying the return to civilian rule.
Transitional President Gen Horta N'Tam announced in a decree that the presidential and parliamentary elections, originally due on 6 December, would now take place on 26 November 2028.
The announcement came exactly a year after the military seized power, promising to return the country to civilian rule within 12 months.
In a statement, the presidency said an assessment of electoral preparations had found that there were insufficient "technical, material and financial conditions" to hold the polls as planned.
It said the delay would provide more time to ensure the elections were credible, transparent and inclusive, with all candidates given equal opportunities.
The presidency also reiterated its commitment to holding the country's first-ever local government elections but gave no date for the vote.
Gen N'Tam was sworn in as transitional president a day after the military overthrew President Umaro Sissoco Embaló in November 2025.
The coup took place three days after general elections and a day before provisional results were due to be announced.
Both Embaló and his main challenger, Fernando Dias, had claimed victory.
Embaló, who has since been living in exile in Morocco, was barred from returning to Guinea-Bissau last month, despite expressing an interest in contesting the elections.
Guinea-Bissau has experienced several coups and attempted coups since gaining independence from Portugal in 1974.

items.text:
India upbeat about first Olympic Games after ‘very good’ 2036 presentation
India makes Ahmedabad pitch for 2036 Games as it bids to host first Olympics, but Qatar and South Africa strong rivals.
Indian officials said they were confident of advancing to the next phase of the race to stage the 2036 Olympic Games after presenting plans for Ahmedabad as the host city.
The Indian Olympic Association (IOA) delivered an online presentation to the International Olympic Committee’s Future Host Commission on Thursday, outlining its vision for staging the mega sporting event in the western city of Ahmedabad.
Ahmedabad, in Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s home state of Gujarat, is already set to host the 2030 Commonwealth Games in a key test of its organisational credentials.
“It was a very, very good presentation that was made,” IOA chief executive Raghuram Iyer told reporters, saying discussions had been held at a “very macro level”.
India is one of seven countries pursuing the 2036 games, alongside Germany, Hungary, Qatar, South Africa, South Korea and Turkiye.
The Indian bid comes after internal disputes within the IOA.
Earlier this month, the IOC warned the association to resolve governance issues, while President P T Usha announced she would not seek re-election in December after alleging a “big fraud” in the nomination process.
Iyer said the bid was in a “continuous dialogue” phase with the IOC, with successful candidates expected to move into a strategic dialogue stage next year.
“We are in this continuous dialogue phase and if you are successful you move onto the stage of strategic dialogue, which will happen in March or April.”
He stressed that hosting an Olympic Games required backing from all levels of government.
“When a country is pitching for the Olympics, doing something so large, it requires the complete support and backing of the city, of the state, of the union.”
A final decision on the 2036 host is not expected until after the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, or in early 2029, he added.

items.text:
Costa Rica denies entry to UN’s Albanese over ‘links to terrorist acts’
Authorities said the UN special rapporteur was blocked from entering the country due to ‘national security’ risks.
Costa Rica has barred United Nations Special Rapporteur on the Occupied Palestinian Territories Francesca Albanese from entering the country, citing “national security” concerns.
Albanese slammed her detention on Friday, branding it a “disgrace”. She was halted and held at Juan Santamaria International Airport the previous day, according to local authorities.
The director-general of Costa Rica’s immigration authority, Omer Badilla, said in a video posted on social media that Albanese “was refused entry to the country because she is the subject of an international alert due to links to terrorist acts”. He did not specify which country put out the alert.
“It is important to note that when national security is at risk, as is the case here, our police authorities strictly enforce the provisions of our legal system,” Badilla said.
Albanese was appointed by the UN Human Rights Council in 2022 and, like other independent experts, does not speak on behalf of the UN. She was travelling to Costa Rica to receive an honorary doctorate from the University of Costa Rica in recognition of academic and human rights work.
She has faced harsh pushback from Israel and its allies, including the United States, over her advocacy for Palestinians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank and accusations that Israel has committed genocide and other war crimes.
Speaking while held at the airport, Albanese told local media that her detention was “a disgrace” and “appalling”.
“You see the face of the empire the day you touch a nerve or cross its boundaries,” she wrote on social media.
The US imposed sanctions on Albanese after she criticised Washington’s policy on Gaza.
Costa Rican President Laura Fernandez is a close ally of US President Donald Trump and has pursued closer trade ties with Israel since she took office in May.
Albanese told the student outlet Semanario Universidad that while she understood her name was on the US sanctions list, that did not explain why Costa Rica had detained her.
“We are not in the United States. We are in Costa Rica,” she stated. “Is Costa Rica a sovereign country?”
She noted that the only country she knew she could not enter was Israel, which had declared her “persona non grata” in 2024.
Danny Danon, Israel’s ambassador to the UN, praised Costa Rica on social media.
“Those who exploit their UN mandate to spread vile propaganda, legitimize terrorist organizations, desecrate the memory of the six million Jews murdered in the Holocaust, and relentlessly vilify the US and Israel should face consequences,” he wrote.

items.text:
‘Will I get taller?’: Gaza’s children suffer stunting amid war, blockade
One in eight children is stunted. Many have bones that have not matured the way they should. And treatment is hard to find – and harder to afford.
Khan Younis, Gaza – Every time seven-year-old Nabigha al-Zaqzouq stands beside children her age, she notices the difference in their heights and asks her mother, Alia: “Will I ever get taller?”
Nabigha is 99cm (3.2ft) tall and weighs just 10kg (22lb), making her appear several years younger than she actually is.
At home, the family’s dining table reflects part of her struggle. Bread and canned food are among the few options available, while meat, fruit and vegetables are beyond the family’s means. Alia tries to provide her daughter with a varied diet but struggles to afford food, as well as the medicines and medical tests needed to monitor her growth.
“We lived through extremely harsh days during the war, and after the ceasefire, we are living under a suffocating blockade. Let them allow medicines and treatments in,” she says. During medical visits, Alia has also started noticing other children with similar growth problems.
Five-year-old Tala Zidan faces a similar struggle. She is 94cm (3ft) tall, about 15-16cm shorter than the average for children her age.
Her father, Tahrir Zidan, says her height has remained almost unchanged over the past two years, while she has lost some weight. Since the family was displaced from Khuza’a to al-Mawasi amid Israel’s genocide, he has lost his job, making food a daily challenge. The family now relies on meals provided by charitable community kitchens.
“I have not been able to buy even one kilogramme (2.2lb) of meat, a chicken or a kilogramme of fruit,” he says. “The meal I get from the community kitchen is usually finished while most of us are still hungry.”
Tala and her brother Mohammed suffer from malnutrition and growth difficulties, as their family cannot afford a healthy diet. Their father fears the deprivation will have lasting consequences for their health.
A crisis beyond food shortages
The experiences of Nabigha and Tala reflect a wider challenge eating away at the future of Gaza’s children. The war has deprived families of adequate food and essential nutrients at a time when healthcare services have been severely disrupted, making access to diagnosis and treatment increasingly difficult.
A nutritional survey by UNICEF and its partners in accessible areas of the Gaza Strip between May 31 and June 15, 2026 found that 12.2 percent of children below five were stunted. Only 22.4 percent of children aged six to 23 months received a minimum acceptable diet.
Nutritionist Nada Abu al-Nada says the crisis concerns not only the quantity of food available, but also its quality and diversity. As purchasing power has declined and prices have risen, many families have reduced their consumption of meat, chicken, fish, eggs, milk, vegetables and fruit, relying increasingly on bread, rice and pasta.
Children need balanced diets containing proteins and essential nutrients, including iron, zinc and calcium, to support bone and muscle development. When they do not receive enough energy and nutrients, the body prioritises vital functions over growth. Prolonged deficiencies can slow height gain and affect muscles, tissues and bone formation.
“Before the war, average food availability was about 2,580 calories per person per day, while estimated average consumption has fallen to approximately 1,000 calories. This is not enough,” Abu al-Nada says.
She explains that the first 1,000 days from conception until a child turns two are particularly critical for development. However, older children are also vulnerable to prolonged deprivation. Diarrhoea, gastrointestinal illnesses and contaminated water can further reduce the body’s ability to absorb nutrients, worsening malnutrition.
Delayed growth and unavailable treatment
At Nasser Hospital, endocrinologist and diabetes specialist Hani Sayed Zuhair has noticed an increase in children seeking medical attention for growth problems. The number of cases during a single clinic session has risen from about 15 to 20 before the war to between 30 and 40 now, sometimes more.
He says the cases indicate an increase in growth disorders and stunting, particularly following periods of hunger and shortages of food, vitamins and medicines.
The consequences extend beyond nutritional deprivation to disrupted diagnosis and treatment, including hormonal therapies required by some children. The effects of malnutrition may not appear immediately but can emerge months or years later.
Zuhair cites cases of eight-year-old children whose bones are at the stage of development normally seen in those half their age, indicating a significant delay in skeletal maturation.
However, he stresses that short stature is not necessarily caused by malnutrition alone. It may also result from hormonal disorders or chronic illnesses, which can be exacerbated by nutritional deprivation, or from a combination of factors.
“We have noticed that many children suffering from malnutrition and short stature also have hormonal deficiencies, but in a number of these cases, the primary problem was nutritional deprivation,” he says.
Diagnosing delayed growth requires monitoring children’s height and weight against growth charts, alongside the necessary medical tests.
But access to diagnosis and treatment is increasingly difficult. Growth hormone stimulation tests are unavailable in Ministry of Health laboratories, while some private laboratories offer them only on a limited basis because of shortages of supplies. According to Zuhair, the tests cost between 350 ($106) and 400 shekels ($120).

items.title: Eagles rally to stun Cowboys coming back from 21 points behind
items.summary:
Eagles rally to stun Cowboys coming back from 21 points behind
ARLINGTON, Texas — Joe Milton rolled to his left while motioning DeVonta Smith where to go near the end zone, then threw the kind of deep ball the Dallas Cowboys always knew he was capable of when he was playing for them.
That 50-yarder
items.text:
Eagles rally to stun Cowboys coming back from 21 points behind
ARLINGTON, Texas — Joe Milton rolled to his left while motioning DeVonta Smith where to go near the end zone, then threw the kind of deep ball the Dallas Cowboys always knew he was capable of when he was playing for them.
That 50-yarder was the first of two long touchdowns for the Philadelphia duo against the quarterback's former team, and the start of quite a comeback.
Milton, who was Dak Prescott's backup all last season, threw three touchdowns and ran for another one in a 39-38 win Thursday in his third start for the Eagles, who signed him off the Dallas practice squad on Oct. 16.
"The guy's a rock star. ... True example of being cool, calm, collected, and just keep playing the next play, no matter what the outcome," said Eagles tackle Jordan Mailata, who was then asked about the long TD passes. "We've seen it in practice a couple of times. The oohs and aahs were still there, but not as much. It was just like you know he can get that throw done."
After 50- and 45-yard touchdown passes to Smith, Milton ran 15 yards for a score in the fourth quarter and threw a 24-yard TD to Makai Lemon with 2:10 left before Philadelphia lined up for a 2-point conversion. Milton connected with Smith in the end zone, but a holding call against Mailata wiped out the tying score before another try was broken up at the goal line.
But the Eagles (4-7), who were down 31-10 early in the third quarter, got one more chance after sacking Prescott on fourth-and-1 for a nine-yard loss to their 48 in the final minute. After a couple of short completions to Smith and a pass interference call against Dallas, Jake Elliott kicked a 59-yard field goal with 2 seconds left.
Milton, signed by the Eagles about the same time they were determining that Jalen Hurts' season was over because of diagnosis of blood clots, completed 21 of 31 passes for a career-best 331 yards.
"You never know when your opportunity is going to come. You never know, when, where, how. The only thing you can do is just prepare yourself," Milton said. "That's just the main thing I did. There wasn't a day where I was in a Cowboys facility and I didn't take notes. I didn't let a day go by where I didn't ask a question. So just being prepared for the moment and I mean, it showed up when it needed to. ... Really trying to hold my emotions in up here. Just thankful for the moment."
While he was sacked five times, and the Cowboys defense had him on the run throughout, Milton made several big plays out of the pocket.
On the 50-yard TD late in the first half, Milton rolled to his left and was in front of the Cowboys sideline when he threw back toward the center of the field — the ball was in the air more than 60 yards before Smith caught it at the goal line. Milton then looked toward the Dallas bench and made some seemingly good-natured gestures with a huge smile on his face.
"Can't even remember doing that, but it was just kind of in a moment," he said.
Then late in the third quarter, while rolling to his right toward his sideline, Milton threw deep to an open Smith, who after the catch had to take only a few steps into the end zone to complete the 45-yard score. Smith had 11 catches for 200 yards.
Milton's quick sprint down the sideline on his touchdown run got the Eagles within 38-30 with 9:09 left.
"He played his butt off. He played really good, made some throws that only he can make," coach Nick Sirianni said. "He played an outstanding game, super composed throughout."
After appearing in four games for Dallas last season, Milton lost his backup role to Sam Howell in training camp this year. But Milton stayed with the Cowboys on their practice squad until getting signed by their NFC East rival.
The Eagles lost their seventh game in a row, 19-11 to the New York Giants in Milton's first start Nov. 8. After a bye week, they won 19-16 last Sunday over Pittsburgh, when Milton got them in range for a field goal and a two-score lead with four minutes remaining and then converted a third down in the final minute that allowed them to run out the clock.
Only one of Milton's regular-season appearances for the Cowboys was at AT&T Stadium, in a 34-17 loss to the Los Angeles Chargers last Dec. 21.
His third start Thursday was only his eighth regular-season game in the NFL after appearing in nine preseason games — six for the Cowboys this season and last, along with three for New England in 2024 after the Patriots drafted him in the sixth round that year.

items.title: France and Germany push for EU budget deal by year-end as far-right rise threatens Ukraine aid
items.summary:
France and Germany push for EU budget deal by year-end as far-right rise threatens Ukraine aid
As Europe braces itself for a slew of tense elections in 2027, Paris and Berlin are pushing for the European Union to strike a budget deal by December 31 to lock in financial aid for Ukraine. But Thursday'
items.text:
France and Germany push for EU budget deal by year-end as far-right rise threatens Ukraine aid
As Europe braces itself for a slew of tense elections in 2027, Paris and Berlin are pushing for the European Union to strike a budget deal by December 31 to lock in financial aid for Ukraine. But Thursday's talks in Brussels seem to have done little to build consensus around the bloc's next budget.
France and Germany want the European Union to reach a deal in the next month on its 2028-2034 budget and financing for Ukraine ahead of a slew of elections across the bloc in 2027, but leaders made little progress on Thursday as discussions grew heated.
While the next EU budget only ‌starts in 2028, leaders want a deal by year-end because France, Italy, Poland, Greece, Estonia, Finland and Slovakia all hold elections next year, which could complicate negotiations on the almost €1.6 trillion ($1.8 trillion) draft budget that pays for all of the EU's key policies.
The seven-year budget requires unanimous approval from all 27 member states.
The possibility that French far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who leads in the polls, becomes president after elections in April ‌and May has focused minds. Le Pen has vowed to end financial aid to Ukraine, which is still fighting to hold back the Russian advance, and slash French contributions to the EU budget.
Deadline approaching
French President Emmanuel Macron told reporters that he had until the end of the year to strike a deal.
"After 31 December, I will no longer be in a position, politically or democratically, to reopen discussions on the budget and bring them to a conclusion, as we will be entering a period far too close to the presidential election in France," Macron said.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz also mentioned the end of the 2026 as the deadline that leaders were ‌working towards.
The talks on Thursday, while inconclusive, are to help the chair of EU summits, Antonio Costa, present a budget proposal in the coming weeks on which EU governments might agree at a meeting on December 17 and 18.
"Even negotiations that do not lead to the desired outcome or the most positive result possible are necessary to make progress," Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker told reporters. "Even though we were apparently ‌unable to bridge our differences today, we may know what is necessary to ensure success next time."
Under the current proposal, the seven-year budget totals €1.582 trillion, which includes €140 billion to repay pandemic-era borrowing. The biggest line item is around €740 billion to support European farmers and help the poorest regions of the EU catch up with the richer ones.
Aid for Ukraine
Leaders must also sort out how to continue financing Ukraine as Kyiv defends itself against a Russian invasion that started in 2022.
The 2028-2034 budget draft includes up to €100 billion for Ukraine, which diplomats say falls well short of the country's needs.
The talks also cover aid to Kyiv in 2027 because a proposed loan intended to raise funds for Ukraine would be borrowed against the EU's current budget, which expires at the end of next year. The EU wants to borrow €45 billion and lend it to Ukraine, to be repaid only when Russia pays war reparations.
In 2027, non-EU countries such as Britain, Norway, Japan, Switzerland and Canada are expected to provide another €25 billion for Ukraine. The combined €70 billion would cover the funding gap that Ukraine faces next year.
Widening divides
One of the fights is over whether all EU countries should contribute to the €45 billion loan to Ukraine.
Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Bulgaria object, but Germany and several other countries have made participation a condition of a broader budget deal.
"For me, there is a link between our support for Ukraine and the European budget," Merz said. "The European Union comprises of 27 member states, not 23 or 24."
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
The four objecting countries are major net beneficiaries of EU spending. The debate is a microcosm of ongoing divisions between countries that contribute more to the EU budget than they get from it, such as Germany, Sweden, the Netherlands and Finland, and those that on balance receive more than they pay.
The net contributors want EU budget reductions, which would lower their contributions, and urge that spending prioritise making the EU more competitive against rivals like the US and China rather than subsidising European agriculture and poor regions.
The net beneficiaries say that the budget should have money for both aims, and believe doing that would sustain public support for the EU in the face of far-right political parties' rising popularity throughout Europe.
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters)

items.title: Millions of wives in South Asia unprotected from marital rape - study
items.summary:
Millions of wives in South Asia unprotected from marital rape - study
- Published
Failure to fully criminalise marital rape leaves millions of women and girls unprotected in eight South Asian countries, where intimate partner violence is 35% higher than the global average, says a new study.
More tha
items.text:
Millions of wives in South Asia unprotected from marital rape - study
- Published
Failure to fully criminalise marital rape leaves millions of women and girls unprotected in eight South Asian countries, where intimate partner violence is 35% higher than the global average, says a new study.
More than 100 countries have outlawed marital rape, but a large part of South Asia - India, Afghanistan, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh - remain among the three dozen countries which haven't.
The only South Asian country where rape within marriage attracts the same penalty as any other rape is The Maldives.
Nepal and Bhutan have criminalised marital rape, but apply lesser penalties, says the study by Samaj, a coalition of women's rights groups in the region.
South Asia's marital rape laws largely stem from British colonial rule, says Ranjeeta Silwal of Equality Now, a global women's rights group part of Samaj.
The law, dating to 1860 in India and Bangladesh and 1885 in Sri Lanka, lists exceptions to rape - including sex by a man with his adult wife.
Campaigners say the law is outdated and forced sex is rape, regardless of the perpetrator. Experts warn marital sexual violence harms women's physical, psychological, emotional and sexual well-being.
More than 100 countries have criminalised marital rape, including the UK, which changed its law in 1991. But the exemption remains in India, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh.
Pakistan removed the marital rape exception in 2006, but no higher court has confirmed that rape laws apply within marriage. A recent high court ruling, meanwhile, granted husbands broad immunity for non-consensual sex.
Since returning to power in 2021, the Taliban have steadily dismantled women's protections in Afghanistan.
A new penal code introduced in January made matters worse, Silwal says. Under it, a husband can be prosecuted for violence against his wife only if he causes a broken bone, open wound or severe bruising. Even then, he faces just 15 days in prison if convicted.
Unsurprisingly, the code makes no mention of marital rape. But its narrow definition of punishable violence effectively denies women protection against it.
"The idea comes from the belief that consent for sex is implied in marriage, that marriage is a threshold where consent ends," Silwal told the BBC.
"But it shows a lack of awareness, it shows we are still treating women as property, that we are still very patriarchal."
The report comes amid renewed debate over marital rape across the region.
In India, 10 petitions challenging the law are pending before the Supreme Court, which is due to begin final hearings on 9 December.
Courts have delivered contradictory rulings over the years, with some judges acknowledging the law's archaic nature and urging parliament to criminalise marital rape.
There was outrage last year when a court let go a man whose wife had died after he brutally raped her.
But the Indian government, religious organisations and men's rights activists have opposed petitions in the top court, saying criminalisation of marital rape would be "excessively harsh".
Rights groups in Bangladesh have also challenged the marital rape exception, arguing it violates constitutional rights to life, liberty and protection from torture and cruel treatment, the report says.
"Those who oppose criminalising marital rape say it would undermine the family unit and break them apart. And family is very important in our countries," Silwal says.
"They say it will affect our religious and cultural values and worry that there would be false accusations against men."
Also a change in law, she says, may not necessarily mean justice for survivors.
Silwal points to Bhutan where marital rape is a criminal offence but it's treated as a petty misdemeanour and is punishable by one month to one year.
In Nepal, the punishment for rape is between six and 20 years, but it's only up to five years for a husband who rapes his wife.

As Jordan Bardella denies fresh allegations concerning antisemitic remarks he allegedly made as a teenager/young adult, how much damage could the affair do to Marine Le Pen's presidential prospects? Ana Navarro Pedro, correspondent for Portuguese media, believes its electoral impact may be limited, despite Le Pen's defence of Bardella and her choice of him as a future prime minister. “What they most regret in this whole episode is that Bardella is denying it,” she says of prospective Le Pen voters.
Navarro suggests that some would have preferred him to acknowledge and express regret for his alleged past remarks. She also examines why accusations of antisemitism appear to have greater repercussions for Jean-Luc Mélenchon, whose electorate, she explains, is particularly sensitive to questions of racism, antisemitism and human rights.
Drawing a parallel between Bardella's denials and Donald Trump's approach, she speaks of “a kind of tribal loyalty” among voters. Politics here are particularly vicious,” Navarro explains, as she considers another possibility: could Le Pen's continued support for Bardella eventually give her grounds to replace him as her prospective prime minister? She also discusses the enduring influence of the Le Pen family within the National Rally and the possibility of another family member rising within the ranks of the party.

items.title: Liam Delap’s struggles are symbolic of damaging Chelsea churn
items.summary: Liam Delap came and went. He joined Chelsea in the summer of 2025 and was hailed by Enzo Maresca as the next Harry Kane. Fast forward a year, though, and there was no chance of Delap joining Kane in England’s World Cup squad. The striker’s form was miserable and the only surprise was that Chelsea ma
items.text:
Liam Delap came and went. He joined Chelsea in the summer of 2025 and was hailed by Enzo Maresca as the next Harry Kane. Fast forward a year, though, and there was no chance of Delap joining Kane in England’s World Cup squad. The striker’s form was miserable and the only surprise was that Chelsea made a profit when they sold him to Nottingham Forest for £50m last summer.
On one level it looks like good business. Delap’s only season at Stamford Bridge featured one serious hamstring injury, one league goal, one ridiculous red card and not much else. Analysts at other clubs rated him at Ipswich and felt Chelsea was the wrong fit for his direct style of play. The mistake was less the decision not to give Delap another season, no matter the worries over cover for João Pedro, more the call to sign him in the first place.
At the same time, however, Delap’s experience speaks to the questions around culture and identity dogging Chelsea before they face Forest and their former striker at the City Ground on Friday night. It is a point that could be applied to so many of the players to join during this ownership’s four years in charge. Alejandro Garnacho, languishing on loan at Aston Villa, was a £40m signing last year, and only three of the 12 players who joined in the 2024-25 season are still at the club.
There is a constant churn. Laurence Stewart has departed the five-strong sporting director team and there also are whispers around Dave Fallows, although insiders insist there will be no further changes. Back to the squad and Moisés Caicedo, Roméo Lavia and Cole Palmer are the only survivors from the 2023-24 intake. Wesley Fofana, Malo Gusto and Gaga Slonina remain from the 16 who joined in the 2022-23 season. The trading is relentless and, although the ability to raise funds meant Chelsea were in position to spend £117m on Morgan Rogers last summer, it is hard not to wonder whether the strategy has hindered the team’s development.
The lack of consistency was evident when Chelsea lost 4-1 at home to Leeds last Saturday. Xabi Alonso, whose side are eighth after five defeats in their first 11 league games, has focused on raising standards. But shifting mindset is harder when the players cannot fall back on a clear identity. The chopping and changing has consequences. Reece James, Chelsea’s captain, is the only first-teamer who represented the club during the Roman Abramovich era. It is not a surprise that supporters feel little connection to the players. Fans wonder whether the long contracts handed out to players have meaning. They hear Fofana appear to joke about missing a penalty against Liverpool and wonder whether the players care. It explains why the atmosphere at Stamford Bridge quickly grows toxic. The culture has to change. There has to be more accountability.
“This is a goal for us – that we are able to have stability, to be more competitive,” Alonso said on Thursday. “For me, to build that core, to build that way of doing things, it’s very important for the newcomers when you really get into the place and you know how things work.”
It is a work in progress. The final whistle against Leeds brought the sight of Palmer, who is horribly out of form, arguing with João Pedro and Willie Isa, the player support and development officer, about refusing to acknowledge the fans. There has been more woe this week, the mood soured by Fofana’s ill-advised chat with a French YouTuber. Fofana has had to apologise after failing to seek club permission for an interview in which he revealed that he almost quit football before his agents pointed out how much money was left on his contract.
Alonso, who refused to say whether the £75m defender had been fined, was unamused. “He apologised,” the manager said. “He knows it was not right. We are here to take things seriously.”
The worry is that Chelsea still look unserious. They have plenty to prove after being bullied by Leeds and Sunderland. Delap, who has been finetuning his heading in training this week, will fancy his chances after Fofana and Levi Colwill toiled against target men when they faced Leeds’ Dominic Calvert-Lewin and Sunderland’s Brian Brobbey.
Confidence in the defence is at rock bottom. Chelsea are not in Europe but Alonso is yet to feel the benefit of extra time on the training ground. His side have conceded 20 goals and keep making silly errors. Jamie Carragher, Alonso’s former teammate at Liverpool, destroyed the pairing of Fofana and Colwill on Sky Sports on this week’s Monday Night Football. They have been exposed by Maxence Lacroix’s hamstring injury. Alonso needs individuals to stop hiding. Chelsea’s midfield crumbled when Caicedo went off injured against Leeds, and the attack has spluttered without João Pedro.
There is no point crying about injuries. Chelsea have spent more than £1bn on their squad. Alonso, who accused his players of failing to perform the basics against Leeds, is yet to make sense of it all and has not instilled a playing identity. He talks about control but it is not clear what he wants Chelsea to be. It is Alonso’s puzzle to solve. Working it out will be easier if Chelsea finally develop some continuity.

items.title: Hull should be in League One, says xG - so how do they keep winning?
items.summary:
Hull City should be in League One this season according to Expected Goals - so how do the Tigers keep winning in the Premier League?
Hull City are sitting comfortably in the middle of the Premier League table - when the Expected Goals underlying data says they should be two divisions below; watch Cr
items.text:
Hull City should be in League One this season according to Expected Goals - so how do the Tigers keep winning in the Premier League?
Hull City are sitting comfortably in the middle of the Premier League table - when the Expected Goals underlying data says they should be two divisions below; watch Crystal Palace vs Hull live on Sky Sports this Sunday from 1pm, kick-off 2pm
Thursday 26 November 2026 14:53, UK
Hull aren't doing much wrong as a newly promoted club so far. A great start to the campaign has them middle of the Premier League table, clear of the relegation zone and unbeaten at home all season.
These are all the right ingredients for survival. But the underlying data says otherwise.
If Expected Goals (xG) decided football matches - yes, yes, we know they don't - then Hull would be bottom of the Premier League, with a similar record to the actual bottom club Crystal Palace, who they play live on Sky Sports this Sunday.
The reason? Hull have only won one game this season on xG since their promotion to the top flight.On its own, this underlying data should be taken with a pinch of salt. xG numbers in a match require context.
For example, a team that loses a game can often end up having a higher xG than the opponent, as they were chasing the game and attacking for longer periods.
- Transfer Centre LIVE! | Hull news & transfers
- Hull fixtures & scores | FREE Hull highlights▶️
- Got Sky? Watch Premier League games LIVE on your phone📱
- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream PL games with no contract📺
The same xG table also has Chelsea in 14th place at the moment. Bournemouth should be third and Nottingham Forest should be sixth. After 11 games, there is a lot of differentiation between the Expected Table and the actual table across the board.
But this isn't a new phenomenon when it comes to Hull. The fascinating thing about the Tigers is that this has been happening for 18 months.
The same xG data says Hull should also be playing in League One this season. That's because last term, they should have finished second-bottom of the Championship after 46 games, according to xG. Instead, they were promoted to the Premier League via the play-offs.
As Aston Villa showed last season, you can get away with overperforming this way for some time but things eventually regress to the mean. To do this over a long period of time is extraordinary.
So why are Hull where they are? Style has something to do with it.
Set up in a 5-4-1 formation, Hull have the lowest possession in the Premier League this season by an absolute country mile. The same applies for the number of shots they have and how high they start pressing up the pitch.
"It is not about possession, it is what you do with it," said manager Sergej Jakirovic told Sky Sports in an interview last month. Hull are comfortable in a low block, which ultimately leads to losing the 'stats side' of games.
So how do Hull actually win games? As their manager says, in the little time Hull get hold of the ball, they use it to good effect - the Tigers move the ball up the pitch quicker than any other team.
There is also an efficiency in attack. In the Championship last season, Hull had two of the most clinical forwards in Ollie McBurnie and Joe Gelhardt. They were given few opportunities, but when they got them, they took them.
The same culture applies here. "No matter who is the opponent, we will have our chances," added Jakirovic.
The aim of the game is not only to progress the ball as quickly as possible, but also choosing the right battles. That can be seen in Hull's pressing.
Hull barely press - they have the lowest number of high turnovers in the Premier League this season. However, they have the second-most goals from high turnovers this season and rank fourth for high pressures that end up in a shot. It's a selective, patient press.
Take their recent draw with Brentford as an example. Their only chance of the first half came from Hull pressing out-of-position midfielder Aaron Hickey to win a penalty which they scored from. Then they relied on the defence to hold out for a result. They conceded late, but got what many would say is a good point.
But this game plan of little possession and reliance on taking advantage of the few attacks that come their way is risky. You need a lot of luck to go your way, and Hull have had their fair share of that.
In the Championship last season, Hull had the most let-offs out of any second-tier team in terms of big chances missed by their opponents. A similar theme has continued in the Premier League.
In Hull's first two home games of the season, Man Utd and Aston Villa should have scored around two goals each, according to xG. Neither of those teams found the net, as the Tigers picked up four points instead.
But it is not just luck. In their most recent home game against Brighton, the performance of Konstantinos Tzolakis caught the eye, which confirms skills matters as well.
The Greek goalkeeper - or 'Greek God' as many Hull fans were claiming last weekend - has the best save record out of any Premier League goalkeeper this season. He alone has prevented nearly 2.0 worth of xG going in.
Without him, and without the game plan from their experienced manager, Hull would be closer to the bottom of the table. Instead, they go to the Premier League's basement club knowing they can still get a result.

items.title: New Zealand election results set up tricky talks for conservative incumbent
items.summary:
New Zealand election results set up tricky talks for conservative incumbent
Conservative PM Luxon and populist coalition partners face negotiations with centrist kingmaker.
The final results of New Zealand’s November 7 election offer no clear path to forming a government, suggesting tricky political
items.text:
New Zealand election results set up tricky talks for conservative incumbent
Conservative PM Luxon and populist coalition partners face negotiations with centrist kingmaker.
The final results of New Zealand’s November 7 election offer no clear path to forming a government, suggesting tricky political wrangling is likely in the weeks ahead.
The results, released on Friday, showed that the ruling centre-right coalition led by Prime Minister Christopher Luxon’s conservative National Party has fallen one seat short of a parliamentary majority.
Luxon has led New Zealand since 2023, but National and its junior partners – the populist New Zealand First and libertarian ACT – won just 65 seats between them. National secured 40 seats while ACT and New Zealand First won 13 seats and 12 seats, respectively.
The result reflects a loss of support for Luxon driven by a stagnant economy, and leaves the former businessman and his coalition partners to seek additional help to secure a majority.
“New Zealanders need a government that is stable, that works together and will last for the full term,” Luxon told a news conference on Friday.
Labour, the largest opposition party, won 36 seats, leaving it far below the 66-seat threshold in the 130-member parliament.
The results appear to position Qiulae Wong’s centrist Opportunity Party, which clinched 7 seats, as kingmaker. However, talks with the conservative and populist incumbents are likely to prove tricky.
The former consultant has promised a universal basic income of up to NZ$370 (US$208) a week, greater action on climate change, a ban on bottom-trawling fishing, and healthcare reforms.
She has also campaigned for a kinder approach to politics. Wong has pledged to do “everything we can” to ensure a stable government.
Her style contrasts with that of potential suitors such as Winston Peters of New Zealand First. The controversial foreign minister has called opponents “morons” and drew shock earlier this year when he told a Chinese-born lawmaker to “go back to your country”. His party promises to tighten immigration flows and withdraw from the Paris Climate Accord.
Deputy Prime Minister David Seymour of ACT campaigned against a greater governance role for the Indigenous Maori minority and has promised massive cuts to state spending.
Failure to meet an agreement could see Kiwis return to the polls next year.
Luke Oldfield, a political scientist at Victoria University of Wellington, told Reuters news agency a deal was likely, although it could be challenging.
“I don’t know exactly what kind of shape that will be yet, but it’ll be highly likely that there will be a right bloc formed and not a second election,” he said.

items.title: ‘Borrowing to make ends meet’: The rising cost of living in Europe
items.summary:
‘Borrowing to make ends meet’: The rising cost of living in Europe
Prices are climbing again across Europe as energy costs surge.
As winter closes in, millions of people across Europe are bracing for another season of rising bills, tighter budgets and hard choices at home.
Inflation in the eurozone
items.text:
‘Borrowing to make ends meet’: The rising cost of living in Europe
Prices are climbing again across Europe as energy costs surge.
As winter closes in, millions of people across Europe are bracing for another season of rising bills, tighter budgets and hard choices at home.
Inflation in the eurozone has climbed to its highest level in three years, as conflict in the Middle East disrupts oil and gas supplies and drives up energy prices, pushing up the cost of everything from heating to the weekly food shop.
Where are prices rising fastest?
In Athens, Giorgos*, a 40-year-old journalist and father of an 11-year-old, says his salary has risen from 800 euros ($878) to 1,100 euros ($1,208) a month over the past two years, but he has not felt the raise.
“Just as before, I’m still borrowing money just to make ends meet,” he said. Even a gyros souvlaki sandwich, long considered Greece’s “people’s food”, now costs more than 4 euros, he added.
His experience is shared across much of Europe, where prices are rising again after two years of relative calm. Inflation in the eurozone has doubled from 2 percent in December 2025 to 4 percent in October 2026, its highest level in three years.
Energy has been the biggest driver, with energy inflation rising to 21 percent in October, its highest level since December 2022, when it was 25.5 percent in the first winter after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, according to Eurostat.
Energy prices have risen far faster than any other category and are pushing up the cost of transport, heating and food.
According to the European Central Bank (ECB) Lithuania (6.1 percent), Bulgaria (5.9 percent) and Greece (5.7 percent) now have the highest inflation rates in the eurozone, adding pressure on households already among the most stretched in the region.
Inflation in Cyprus jumped from 0.1 percent at the end of last year to 5.4 percent, and in Italy from 1.2 percent to 5.6 percent.
Prices have also accelerated quickly in Belgium, where inflation rose from 2.2 percent to 5.2 percent, and in France, where it rose from 0.7 percent to 3.7 percent.
A handful of countries have bucked the trend. Between December 2025 and October 2026, inflation has eased in Slovakia (from 4.1 percent to 2.9 percent), Estonia (3.6 percent), Latvia (3.1), Austria (3.5) and Malta (2.3), setting Lithuania apart from its Baltic neighbours.
The current rise is still well below the peak that followed the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine, but for many families it is a second shock before they have fully recovered from the first.
How much more expensive has life become?
In North London, Emma*, 33, who works in corporate governance and lives alone, says the cost of food and bills keeps rising, with rent “the biggest killer”.
She has cancelled streaming subscriptions and switched to a cheaper brand of cat food for her pet cat after the one she always purchased started putting less in each can at a higher price.
She now sees her friends less, because nearly 10 pounds ($13) for a return Tube journey is “ridiculous”.
“I think this is detrimental to our mental health and has exacerbated the loneliness epidemic,” she said.
She’s not alone in feeling she has to make choices to survive. This squeeze is being felt across Europe.
According to Eurostat, a typical basket of goods and services such as food, housing, energy and transport now costs 69 percent more than it did in 2000, and around two-fifths of that increase has come in just the past four years.
The sharpest rise came in 2022, when prices jumped by more than 8 percent in a single year as energy costs soared after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The steepest increases have been in Central and Eastern Europe.
Prices in Hungary have more than tripled since 2000, meaning the goods and services that cost 100 euros ($115) in 2000 now cost about 335 Euros ($385), with a surge of 17 percent in 2023 alone. Estonia and Latvia are not far behind.
How difficult is it to find a job?
Finding work in Europe is far easier than it was a decade ago, but in many countries it has been getting harder again since 2022.
According to Eurostat, southern Europe has seen the biggest turnaround.
At the height of the eurozone debt crisis in 2013, unemployment reached 27.8 percent in Greece and 26.1 percent in Spain, meaning more than a quarter of people looking for work could not find a job.
Unemployment in both countries has fallen steadily since then as their economies recovered, to 8.9 percent in Greece and 10.5 percent in Spain in 2025, although Spain still has the highest rate in the EU.
The picture has shifted in northern Europe, where unemployment has risen since 2022 as economies slowed.
Unemployment in Finland has climbed to 9.7 percent in 2025, giving it the second-highest jobless rate in the bloc, ahead of Greece (8.9 percent) and Sweden (8.8 percent).
How much room do governments have to help?
When prices rise, people often look to their governments for financial support. But how much help a government can provide depends partly on how much debt it already carries.
The debt-to-GDP ratio compares a country’s total government debt with the value of everything its economy produces in a year. A ratio of 100 percent means the government owes as much as the economy produces in a year. The higher the ratio, the more money the government may have to spend on interest payments, leaving less available to help households.
Emma believes governments are spending in the wrong places. “Stop using taxpayer money to subsidise high energy bills while fossil fuel and grid companies continue making record profits,” she said, calling for windfall tax loopholes to be closed so those profits fund household relief directly.
According to data from International Monetary Fund (IMF), Italy and Greece carry the heaviest debts in Europe, each owing well over a year’s worth of economic output.
France, Ukraine, Belgium and the UK also owe more than their economies produce in a year.
