items.text:
Chelsea Q&A: Your questions answered on Wesley Fofana, transfers, Danny Welbeck, Estevao and more
Your questions answered by Sky Sports News' James Savundra on Chelsea's season, with Blues having lost three of last four in Premier League; Wesley Fofana’s unauthorised interview, the absences of Danny Welbeck and Estevao, and January transfer plans all addressed
Thursday 26 November 2026 17:56, UK
After Chelsea fell to back-to-back losses with a 4-1 humiliation by Leeds at Stamford Bridge last Saturday, Sky Sports News reporter James Savundra examines the latest developments at Stamford Bridge.
As well as suffering a third defeat in four Premier League games, Chelsea and manager Xabi Alonso also faced the added frustration of defender Wesley Fofana giving an unauthorised interview this week, in which he laughed off his penalty miss in last month's Carabao Cup defeat to Liverpool and revealed he had contemplated retiring during his time at Stamford Bridge.
Here, Savundra addresses Fofana's future, Joao Pedro's injury, transfer plans and much more...
- Transfer Centre LIVE! | Chelsea news & transfers🔵
- Chelsea fixtures & scores | FREE Chelsea highlights▶️
- Got Sky? Watch Premier League games LIVE on your phone📱
- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream PL games with no contract📺
Will Fofana face disciplinary action?
Jake: Is Fofana expected to face any disciplinary action for his impromptu interview? Some of the things said in that were unacceptable from a footballer, especially one involved in as much off-the-pitch controversy as him.
James says: Xabi Alonso addressed this at Thursday's press conference. Fofana has apologised following the interview. The matter has been dealt with internally and there are no suggestions that the defender is set to miss any matches.
Whether the club look to punish Fofana with a fine is not known at this stage. Alonso made clear that this will not be repeated. It's completely understandable to emphasise with Chelsea supporters. Fofana simply hasn't justified the £75m that Chelsea paid Leicester City.
Why is he still in the team?
Benny: Why is Fofana still being chosen when every single fan watching football can see how poor his form is?
James says: At the moment there is a lack of real alternative options. Xabi Alonso stood behind the Fofana-Colwill axis during Thursday's press conference despite their clear struggles dealing with Dominic Calvert-Lewin and Brian Brobbey.
Liam Delap will prove a similar physical threat tomorrow [Friday] with an added point to prove. Ultimately, Chelsea trimmed down their squad in the summer in light of no European football. Maxence Lacroix would be starting, possibly ahead of Fofana right now if he was fit.
Colwill has found things difficult this season having missed the majority of the last campaign. In hindsight, should Chelsea have sold Trevoh Chalobah? Perhaps it was time for the academy graduate to end his Chelsea chapter but he rarely let the side down.
You could feasibly play Josh Acheampong at centre-back. The youngster has been a shining light this season. Yet he looks comfortable on the right. Do you want to upset something which actually seems to be working. And if Acheampong moves to centre-back, then does Marco Palestra play as a right-back?
The Italian impressed in Serie A as a wing-back but with Chelsea opting largely for a flat back four, is Palestra defensively good enough to fulfil that role. Aaron Anselmino remains an option but hasn't played a minute for the club this season.
Will Chelsea invest in January?
Mikey: Will Chelsea sell and buy any defenders and strikers in January? I feel we need stronger defenders with a better aerial ability and maybe a more out and out No 9 to challenge Joao Pedro and give us something different.
James says: Chelsea will spend money in January if they believe it will help them achieve their target this season - qualifying for the Champions League. They were pleased with what they did in the summer but accept that the squad still requires investment.
It seems unlikely any defenders will be sold given the lack of current options. A loan move would seem to suit Aaron Anselmino given his lack of options. The winter window is a difficult one. There's a sense that Chelsea could benefit from signing a more experienced centre-back, considering the moves for Emi Martinez, Jordan Henderson and Danny Welbeck in every other area of the pitch in the summer.
The club have shown a willingness to tweak their transfer model and sign players for the here and now, in addition to targeting players for the future. A striker would appear unlikely given the presence of Emmanuel Emegha and Danny Welbeck. It will be interesting to watch Emegha's development if given a run of games in the absence of Joao Pedro.
The fact that Xabi Alonso opted for a false nine in three matches prior to Leeds would suggest he believes there are shortcomings in both Emegha and Welbeck's games. It feels more likely that Chelsea will revisit the forward line next summer.
How has Joao Pedro's injury affected Chelsea?
JD: How has Joao Pedro's injury affected how Chelsea has been playing as an overall team, and how has Xabi Alonso had to adapt to it?
James says: The stats are undeniable. Since the start of last season, Chelsea average 1.8 goals per game when Joao Pedro plays, compared to 0.6 when he doesn't. It's quite staggering the difference that the Brazilian seems to make.
Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers look far more potent when they are playing off him. Danny Welbeck initially started in his absence at Brentford. However, he had virtually no impact and appears to have fallen down the pecking order.
Playing Rogers or Pedro Neto as a false-nine has been experimented with but Chelsea have looked blunt without a focal point - though Emmanuel Emegha scored in his first Premier League start which was really encouraging.

A LILLE SPOT OF BOTHER
Bayern Munich’s 2-1 defeat to Lille was arguably the most eye-catching of Wednesday night’s Bigger Cup results, but anyone who tuned into proceedings at Stade Pierre-Mauroy will have been unsurprised by the outcome. Not so much an elite European tie as a game of Name That Baye
items.text:
A LILLE SPOT OF BOTHER
Bayern Munich’s 2-1 defeat to Lille was arguably the most eye-catching of Wednesday night’s Bigger Cup results, but anyone who tuned into proceedings at Stade Pierre-Mauroy will have been unsurprised by the outcome. Not so much an elite European tie as a game of Name That Bayern Reserve, the German champions’ starting lineup resembled a pale facsimile of its usual self. Their current knack-list includes such high-profile names as – deep breath – Harry Kane, Michael Olise, Alphonso Davies, Manuel Neuer, Serge Gnabry, Luis Díaz, Jamal Musiala and Ismael Saibari. And with Díaz and Musiala only fit enough for places on the bench, Konrad Laimer was deployed as a makeshift striker. The veteran right-back is famously as handy as a small pot, but filling Kane’s iconic Skechers proved a task too far for the Austrian.
Lille’s winner came from a similarly unlikely source of goals for the French side, with Aleksandar Pavlovic popping up to score a hilarious own goal that left his Bayern teammates giving him the collective stink-eye as he sank to his knees, head in hands in the traditional mea culpa style. Having seen Ethan Mbappé played clean through courtesy of a lightning-fast Lille counterattack, Pavlovic sprinted back towards his own team’s goal like a cheating spouse who’s just realised they left their phone unlocked on the coffee table. Although his panicked chase looked to be in vain, the German hit pay-dirt when Mbappé rolled his low shot past Bayern goalkeeper Jonas Urbig, only to see it rebound off the foot of the post. Cue Pavlovic, who accidentally stabbed the ball into the gaping goal as he attempted what appeared to be the routine task of putting it out for a corner.
While Pavlovic’s own goal was definitely the funniest Bayern have scored in recent memory, it certainly wasn’t the most embarrassing. That dubious honour goes to assorted club blazers including Karl-Heinz Rummenigge, Uli Hoeness and Jan-Christian Dreesen, who have publicly questioned whether Musiala is worth the astronomical wages he is paid, given his struggles with knack and recent diagnosis with a treatable neurological disorder. Rummenigge even went so far as to suggest that if the 23-year-old does not return to top form, the remaining four years of his contract would “no longer be justifiable” and suggested a pay cut might be in order. Asked about this tone-deaf and decidedly mercenary invasion of his teammate’s medical privacy by club officials, Joshua Kimmich gave his superiors both barrels. “What I don’t understand is the way this is being communicated in public,” he harrumphed. “It must never happen that the burden is placed on a player. The club is obviously the top priority and bigger than a player, but it’s not bigger than a person. That’s an absolute no-go and it is not Bayern-like.” Neither is the shame of being second in the Bundesliga while languishing in 15th place in Bigger Cup Monster Group, but don’t expect anyone in the club boardroom to volunteer to trim their wages accordingly.
LIVE ON BIG WEBSITE
Join Will Unwin from 8pm for hot Big Vase action, including Sunderland 2-1 Jagiellonia, Torreense 1-1 Celtic and Crystal Palace 1-1 Real Sociedad, plus reaction from Celta Vigo 0-1 Bournemouth, Brighton 3-0 Universitatea Craoiva and Hearts 0-3 Monaco.
QUOTE OF THE DAY
“Stability in a company is having standards. Everybody who joins commits to the standards. I think, very honestly, the standards were not high enough. We have players who are here for four years, [who] can’t speak English. If you go to Italy, after three months, every player gives his interview in the Italian language. For me, if I want to manage in England, I have to speak English” – Oliver Glasner puts his Nottingham Forest squad’s linguistic skills on blast.
FOOTBALL DAILY LETTERS
 
 I liked Erling Haaland’s observation that football can simultaneously be “easy and difficult” [yesterday’s Football Daily]. That got me thinking about other things that have conflicting characteristics. Soup can be both sweet and sour. My feelings for my partner often run hot and cold. And my daily tea-timely newsletter can be mildly funny and mildly unfunny – Mike Wilner.
 
 The constant change in Watford manager, a once fine club whose first two managers lasted a total of 23 years, is now so high that I don’t even notice it anymore ... apparently this was yesterday, and I’ve no idea who the previous bloke was. Watford are now onto their 30th manager, including caretakers, although in practice they’re all just caretaker managers, since the Pozzos took over in 2012. I don’t know whether to laugh at, or cry for, the Watford fans (Narrator: it’s the former, obviously) – Noble Francis.
If you have any, please send letters to the.boss@theguardian.com. Today’s prizeless letter o’ the day goes to … Mike Wilner. Terms and conditions for our competitions, when we run them, are here.

items.text:
Egyptian authorities arrest motorist over tanker crash that killed 31
- Published
Egyptian authorities have arrested a man accused of causing a tanker crash and massive fire that killed 31 people on a busy Cairo highway.
The public prosecutor's office said the motorist had confessed to driving at 110km/h (68mph) along a section of ring road, to the north of the old city centre, and clipping the tanker with the side of his car as he changed lanes.
Sources close to the investigation were earlier quoted by state media as saying a high-voltage cable had fallen in front of the fuel truck, causing the driver to lose control.
Twenty-one others were injured in the crash in the Warraq neighbourhood on Wednesday evening, with hospitals treating patients for burns and smoke inhalation.
The public prosecutor's office said on Thursday that "upon questioning the suspect and confronting him with the findings of the investigation... he confessed to committing the act".
"He added that, while moving between traffic lanes and overtaking vehicles, the left side of his car collided with the right rear side of the tanker. This caused him to lose control of the steering wheel and his car veered to the far right of the road."
At the same time, one of the fuel tanker's tyres burst, causing it to veer into the highway's central reservation, hit the concrete barrier and overturn, spilling fuel and igniting a fire, the prosecutor's office said.
Egyptian authorities have not named the suspect accused of causing the fatal crash, but they said he had been travelling with his father at the time.
The raised motorway - a major artery for traffic around the Egyptian capital - was reopened by emergency services hours after the crash occurred, with the burnt-out wrecks of cars shifted to the side by bulldozers and diggers.
A cabinet minister said on Thursday that 10 million Egyptian pounds (£139,000; $182,000) had been donated to the families of the victims, while the nation's sports minister said all state-run celebratory activities would be cancelled in the aftermath of the crash.
Egypt has suffered several deadly fires in recent years. Road collisions are also common, attributed to poor maintenance and violations of traffic laws, and leading to thousands of road deaths a year.

items.title: Euro-Office comes to your desktop with the Nextcloud Office Desktop app

With Nextcloud Hub 26 Summer, we announced the release of the Nextcloud Office Desktop app powered by Euro-Office. Today, the ready-to-use version
items.text:
On June 9, 2026, we released the first production-ready version of Euro-Office, a sovereign collaborative office suite developed and governed in Europe. With Nextcloud Hub 26 Summer, we announced the release of the Nextcloud Office Desktop app powered by Euro-Office. Today, the ready-to-use version of the app is available for download. It lets you work offline, switch between Nextcloud Hub in your browser and the app on your computer, and get the same experience on Windows, macOS and Linux.
In this article, you’ll learn about the app’s features, how to install it on Windows, macOS and Linux, and how to co-edit files with your team through Nextcloud Hub.
Free desktop office with maximum file compatibility
The Nextcloud Office Desktop app is a free and open source office suite for Windows, macOS and Linux. Featuring editors for text documents, spreadsheets, presentations, and PDFs, it offers high compatibility with Microsoft Office formats (DOCX, XLSX, PPTX) and open formats (ODT, ODS, ODP). Connect it to Nextcloud Hub to edit files with your team in real time.
The app includes the features of Nextcloud Office in your browser, plus the benefits of working on your computer:
- Work offline and keep files on your device
- Use the fonts installed on your computer
- Sign documents digitally
Work with local and online files
With the Nextcloud Office Desktop app, you can edit files locally without an internet connection. Working locally, you keep access to your files and you can keep working when you don’t have internet connection or your online tools go down. You decide which files stay on your computer and which go to the cloud.
Need to access your online files? You can connect your Nextcloud instance to the Nextcloud Office Desktop app to access all the files available to you, and edit them on your own or with your team in real time.
How to connect the Nextcloud Office Desktop app to the cloud:
- Click “+” in the “Clouds” section in the Home tab
- Choose “Nextcloud“ and specify the URL of your instance
- Log in with your credentials
Once connected, choose your Nextcloud instance from the list. You can connect more than one instance to one app to have access to multiple cloud working environments.
Use your own fonts
The Nextcloud Office Desktop app uses fonts installed on your machine, including corporate fonts and default fonts from your OS, like Microsoft fonts on Windows. You can install additional custom fonts any time. No need to bother your Nextcloud admins!
Note: if your collaborators don’t have the same font, they’ll see a fallback font in their version of the file.
Digital signatures and file protection
The Nextcloud Office Desktop app lets you use digital signatures to sign your documents, spreadsheets and presentations. A signature shows who signed a file and that nobody has changed it since. Go to Protection tab and add a signature via Signature feature.
Keep in mind that you need a digital certificate to sign documents. To obtain one, you can ask your IT team at work, or get one for personal use from a trusted provider. You can find providers approved in the EU in this list.
In the Protection tab, you can also set a password for a file, or limit what others can do: comment, fill in forms, or edit with tracked changes only.
How to install the Euro-Office desktop app
You can find and download the latest version of the Nextcloud Office Desktop app from our official installation page.
The app is available for:
- Windows: x64, ARM64
- Linux: .deb (Debian, Ubuntu), .rpm (Fedora)
- macOS (Apple Silicon)
You can also find unsigned builds of Euro-Office desktop app and build the app from the source yourself by following the instructions on GitHub.
We want to keep improving the app. You are welcome to share any issues you find with our engineering team on GitHub.
Want to contribute to Euro-Office? Here’s how to get involved
Contributions are welcome! Whether it’s a bug report, a feature idea, a translation, or a pull request, here’s how to take part:
- Found a bug or have an idea? Open an issue and describe what you ran into or what you’d like to see.
- Want to contribute code? Fork the relevant component repo, make your change, and open a pull request. For build changes, see the build docs.
- Want to help translate? Localization improvements are always appreciated — see the editors’ interface translations.
Please keep contributions compatible with the project’s AGPL v3 license.

items.title: Intel One Mono font

items.text:
Introducing Intel One Mono, an expressive monospaced font family that’s built with clarity, legibility, and the needs of developers in mind.
It’s easier to read, and available for free, with an open-source font license.
Identifying the typographically underserved low-vision developer audience, Frere-Jones Type designed the Intel One Mono typeface in partnership with the Intel Brand Team and VMLY&R, for maximum legibility to address developers' fatigue and eyestrain and reduce coding errors. A panel of low-vision and legally blind developers provided feedback at each stage of design.
Intel One Mono also covers a wide range of over 200 languages using the Latin script. The Intel One Mono fonts are provided in four weights — Light, Regular, Medium, and Bold — with matching italics, and we are happy to share both an official release of fonts ready to use as well as editable sources.
To install the fonts, please use the provided builds under Releases. Please refer to your software’s documentation for how to activate and use these fonts.
- VSCode - In Settings, search Font Family, then specify Intel One Mono
- Sublime Text - Go to Sublime Text -> Preferences -> Settings and set font_face to Intel One Mono
- IntelliJ Platform - Go to File -> Settings -> Editor -> Font and set Font to Intel One Mono
- We recommend the .otf or .ttf format for desktop use.
- The .ttf files are also well suited for mobile apps.
- The .woff and .woff2 fonts are optimized for web use.
We recommend using these fonts at 7 points and larger in print, 9 pixels and larger on screen. The .ttf, .woff and .woff2 fonts provided in the official release have been manually optimized for screen display, improving clarity and legibility, especially on Windows platforms.
Outside of the default characters, there are a few extra features that are accessible in some applications, as well as via CSS:
- Programming Ligatures: To use programming ligatures, activate the ss01 feature (Stylistic Set #1). Additional refinements are available via ss02 and ss03: Stylistic Set #2 switches the <= and >= combinations to arrow forms (math contractions being the default otherwise), and Stylistic Set #3 additionally activates a “www” ligature.
- Alternate three: New in release 1.5. Alternate form for three added. The round top three, numerator, denomenator, superior and inferior can be activated with stylistic Set #4.
- Raised Colon: The colon is automatically raised in operators, to align with math symbols. For non-programming contexts, the raised colon can be applied contextually between numbers or activated generally. The contextual option is available via ss11 (Stylistic Set #11); for the global switch use ss12 (Stylistic Set #12) or salt (Stylistic Alternates).
- Language Support: ccmp and locl features ensure correct display across a wide range of languages. These are usually active by default. We recommend setting the language tag/setting in your software to the desired language for best results.
- Superior/superscript and inferior/subscript figures are included via their Unicode codepoints, or you can produce them from the default figures via the sups (Superscript) and subs/sinf (Subscript) features.
- Fraction numerals are similarly available via the numr (Numerator) and dnom (Denominator) features. A set of premade fractions is also available in the fonts.
Programming ligatures are not active by default. To use them, activate the stylistic sets of your preference in your code editor. For example:
- VSCode - In Settings, add "editor.fontLigatures": "'ss01'"
- Sublime Text - In Settings, add "font_options": ["ss01"]
You will find editable sources in the sources directory. The instances subfolder contains separate source files for each style of the typeface. Sources are provided in .ufo files, which contain complete artwork, links to OpenType features provided in separate .fea files, as well as meta information like naming and vertical alignments for each style of the typeface.
These are not installable fonts, but rather the source files that produce them: UFO (Unified Font Object) is an open, human-readable font source file format; you can find the file spec here. These sources were created using RoboFont. Many other font editors will also be able to open .ufo files; we recommend using RoboFont version 4.4.
For instances, you will find postscript and truetype subfolders; these contain separate source files for the .otf format and the .ttf/.woff/.woff2 files respectively. Since the format for the outline drawings differs between these sets of formats, for best results we recommend using the postscript sources to create .otf fonts, and the TrueType sources to create .ttf, .woff, or .woff2 fonts.
After making your desired edits, you can generate installable fonts directly from the font editor using its “Generate Font” functionality. If you use RoboFont, any install options should default to the ideal settings, but here they are for reference:
- For .otf builds, we recommend activating “Decompose” as well as “Autohint” options.
- For .ttf, .woff and .woff2 builds, we recommend activating the “Autohint” option only (see note on hinting below).
- In any case, we recommend using the “Release Mode” setting for best results.
If you would like to apply edits across multiple weights, a more advanced yet potentially efficient way is to edit the masters. These are special sources that describe the extreme points in the design space — the lightest and heaviest weights for both roman and italic designs.
After editing masters, you will need to rerun interpolation to generate individual weights and styles within that design space. This requires the .designspace files enclosed with the masters. The designspace format is an open, XML-based format that describes interpolation spaces (format specification for reference). For a RoboFont-based workflow we recommend Skateboard for interpolation; you can also use the free DesignSpaceEditor extension to view and edit

items.summary: A coalition of 42 state attorneys general is trying to prevent Character.AI from selling off user data as it navigates Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceedings. In a deluge of nearly identical press releases, the various AGs accuse the company of planning to auction off “the private chat histories of more
items.text:
A coalition of 42 state attorneys general is trying to prevent Character.AI from selling off user data as it navigates Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceedings. In a deluge of nearly identical press releases, the various AGs accuse the company of planning to auction off “the private chat histories of more than 21 million U.S. accounts — more than 2.1 million of them registered to minors — with no safeguards for the people whose conversations are being sold.”
42 state AGs are trying to stop Character.AI from selling users’ chats
A bipartisan coalition of AGs say Character.AI is planning to sell the personal data of minors to the highest bidder.
In October, Character.AI filed for bankruptcy following years of scandals and legal challenges, including from Disney. Disney ended up buying some of the company’s assets and hiring its CEO, Karandeep Anand, in a sort of “acquihire” arrangement that will also see “a number of Character.AI’s technical team” join the entertainment giant. The Disney deal also faced opposition from a similarly broad coalition of AGs.
The main point of contention with Character.AI’s plan to sell its chat data is that it offers no protections for users. The AGs say there are no requirements that the buyer honor existing privacy policies, no avenues for users to delete their data, and no inherent limits on what a buyer could do with that data, including selling it on to yet another party. It doesn’t help that the first bidder has a limited paper trail, having only been established on November 13th, 2026, with no parent company or investors listed.
Some states, including New York, Connecticut, California, and Colorado, have also passed laws regulating chatbots that Character.AI may be in violation of when they go into effect on January 1st, 2027.

items.title: Google Will Make AI Agents Use Its MCP Servers. The Gmail One Can't Send Email
items.summary:
Google Will Make AI Agents Use Its Workspace MCP Servers. The Gmail One Can't Send Email
On 24 November, Google made its eight Workspace MCP servers generally available and published a new clause in its API terms. From 1 February 2027, any tool that "is or is driven by an AI Agent" must reach Gmail,
items.text:
Google Will Make AI Agents Use Its Workspace MCP Servers. The Gmail One Can't Send Email
On 24 November, Google made its eight Workspace MCP servers generally available and published a new clause in its API terms. From 1 February 2027, any tool that "is or is driven by an AI Agent" must reach Gmail, Drive, Calendar and the rest of Workspace through those servers.
Read the Gmail server's tool list and you'll find that it can search your mail, read threads, create a draft and file things under labels. It can't send a message, reply, forward, or change a draft after creating it. Those tools exist, but Google's quota page says they "require partner access and aren't generally available".
If you've built an email assistant on the Gmail API, or you run a coding agent with a Google Workspace plugin, you have about two months to work out which side of the rule you're on.
What the rule says
The new Workspace AI Tools Addendum to the Google APIs Terms of Service puts it in one sentence:
The GWS Access Tool must use a Google MCP where the GWS Access Tool is or is driven by an AI Agent, an AI Harness or an AI model or service employing an AI model.
The next sentence forbids disguising an agent to avoid the classification. Breaking either lets Google "restrict or remove the GWS Access Tool's access" or suspend your account.
There's a technical side too. From the same date, agents that call the REST APIs directly are held to Standard-tier quotas, whatever tier the project has paid for. REST keeps working for them, slowly and in breach of the terms.
Apps that don't involve AI carry on as before. A nightly backup job, a CRM sync or a deterministic script on its own OAuth client is, in Google's words, "not affected by this change".
The addendum also adds data rules that matter to anyone building an agent with memory:
- Workspace data may only be processed "to fulfill active, user-authorized tasks", and must be deleted when the user disconnects.
- Google can cap retention of what it calls "Google Technical Information" at 30 days. Its definition includes vector embeddings, memory indexes, user profiles and organisational graphs built from Workspace data.
- Training, fine-tuning, evals and distillation on the data are banned, as is using it to build a competing Workspace product.
The 30-day cap is the one product teams will feel. An assistant that builds a long-term index of your inbox to answer questions about last year's contracts has to rebuild it monthly or drop it.
What the MCP servers can do
Coverage is uneven. Docs, Slides and Tasks are close to everything the REST API offers. Gmail and Drive are much thinner.
The Gmail gap is the one that breaks real workflows. An agent that drafts a reply, gets feedback from you and revises it before you hit send can't do the revision step. It has to create a second draft and leave the first one behind.
Drive's gap is similar: an agent can create a report but can't move it into the right folder or share it with the team.
Partners get more
Google hasn't said who qualifies for partner access or when the partner-only Gmail tools will reach everyone. The effect is already visible, though. Anthropic's Google Workspace connector for Claude advertises sending, replying and forwarding email, and moving and trashing Drive files. Those are exactly the operations the public servers lack.
So a large AI vendor's agent can send your email through an approved channel, while an independent developer's agent, using the same OAuth scopes the user granted, can only leave drafts. Once the addendum takes effect, that independent developer also can't fall back to the REST API without breaching the terms.
Who counts as an agent
The definitions are broad. An "AI Harness" or a tool "driven by" an AI model plausibly covers a personal script that pipes your inbox into an LLM, and a "GWS Access Point" explicitly includes any "connector, proxy, command line interface, or third-party service". Google hasn't addressed hobby use directly.
Classification starts with self-declaration. OAuth clients now have a checkbox, "Use this client for an AI-powered agent", and since 11 November the MCP servers reject clients without it. Clients created before the cut-off and not marked in time stay non-agentic permanently, so owners have to create new ones. Google hasn't said how it will detect agents that call REST without declaring themselves.
A few edge cases are documented:
- Service accounts with domain-wide delegation can't set the agentic flag. Their MCP requests aren't rejected for missing it, but still trigger approval prompts.
- Apps Script's built-in OAuth client can't be marked as agentic either. Scripts that call the MCP servers need a custom client, and scripts that don't call them aren't affected.
- The community gws CLI, which wraps the entire REST surface, keeps working. Its README now points agent use to Google's new official CLI, gwscli, which offers "a curated set of commands designed for agents" and needs the MCP services enabled.
Quotas and pricing
Every project gets the free Standard tier: 5,000 MCP requests per day, per project, per product. Some calls cost more than one request. A Gmail search_threads or list_drafts counts as 10, so an agent that does nothing but search gets 500 searches a day across all its users. That's a project-wide limit, so a small multi-user product will hit it quickly.
The paid Scaled tier starts billing on 1 April 2027 for Gmail, Calendar and Drive. Its structure favours REST. MCP usage is billed from the first request, while REST usage gets large free daily allowances: 70 million light Gmail requests a day, for example. Google hasn't published per-request prices.
Google's reasoning
Google's case, from a Cloud blog post by Chandu Thota and Brad Calder, is that OAuth was designed for apps acting on a human's clear intent:
Traditional REST APIs were built for human-paced apps where a valid OAuth token implied user intent. As AI agents shift from reading informa

items.text:
Guinea orders residents to clean up the capital months after deadly rubbish dump collapse
- Published
Guinea has ordered residents to do a mass clean-up of the capital, Conakry, months after a rubbish landfill collapsed, killing dozens of people.
Prime Minister Amadou Oury Bah on Wednesday announced a deadline of 31 December to clear rubbish in the city and its suburbs, which has seen an increase in illegal dumping in recent months.
In August heavy rains caused a landslide at the capital's main waste dump, with the rubbish collapsing onto homes killing 31 people and injuring others.
The site in the city's Dar es Salaam area was subsequently closed permanently, which has led to piles of rubbish accumulating outside homes and on the streets.
At a public forum on sanitation, Sanitation Minister Aboubacar Camara said Conakry was generating about 3,000 tonnes of waste every day.
He said much of the garbage was ending up in the streets because of weaknesses in the collection system.
The prime minister called on local authorities to become more involved in organising waste collection, saying this could become a way to create jobs.
"The state will do its part, but the municipalities must also organise themselves to ensure waste collection and provide jobs for young people," the prime minister said.
"Conakry must be completely clean by the end of December," he added, relaying a directive from the country's president, Mamady Doumbouya.
He cited measures the government was taking to improve waste collection and recycling, including a national sanitation fund that would guarantee financing for the sector.
Camara said talks had been finalised with a waste collection operator, with a plan for equipment to move waste from transit and sorting centres to a new disposal site in Baretodé, outside the capital.
The August tragedy at the Dar es Salaam landfill was not the first - 10 people were killed at the same site in 2017.
The government had ordered people living close to the site to move, but many residents chose to stay.
According to the prime minister, the government now plans to transform the closed waste site into an urban park.

items.text:
OpenAI may be in cost control mode
OpenAI’s recent release of Astra 6.2 and Sol 6.2 was widely panned. What happened?
Based on our data, it looks like they’ve been tuned for cost savings. Specifically output tokens per task and reasoning tokens per task have dropped.
Here is a chart of high-level cost change from the GPT-6 to GPT 6.2:
The X axis in the above chart is the ratio of spending of the GPT model compared to opponents in our battle system for real work. The Y axis on the above chart is Elo from our leaderboard.
The moves in the chart are significant, here’s the same chart with confidence intervals:
What changed
Compared to opponents, Astra and Sol seem to be reasoning a lot less. Here is a chart of how much models reason compared to opponents in the same battle. Above the line means more reasoning and below means less.
You can see that both Astra 6 and Sol 6.1 were pretty normal models, but Astra 6.2 and Sol 6.2 become outliers.
We can see the same effect with output tokens:
Are these changes significant? The p-value on output dropping is 0.0055 for Sol and 0.022 for Astra. The p-value on reasoning dropping is 0.00013 for Sol and 0.0064 for Astra.
In conclusion, Astra and Sol appear to be cost tuned compared to their predecessors, and to a degree that makes them underthinking outliers.

items.text:
DR Congo demands answers over Ugandan general's threats
- Published
The Democratic Republic of Congo has summoned Uganda's top diplomat in Kinshasa over social media posts by Uganda's military chief, Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who is also the president's son.
In a series of X posts, Gen Kainerugaba appeared to support a rebel takeover of Walikale, a mineral-rich territory in eastern DR Congo. He insisted that Uganda's military involvement was purely driven by security concerns.
The DR Congo's foreign ministry summoned Uganda's envoy to explain the remarks, describing them as "particularly serious" and damaging to diplomatic relations.
The Ugandan government has yet to respond.
The diplomatic row comes despite close military ties between the neighbours.
Their forces have been conducting joint operations against the Islamic State-linked Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) in eastern DR Congo since 2021.
Uganda has also recently been involved in efforts to mediate between the Congolese government and an armed group led by former warlord Thomas Lubanga in Ituri province.
- The Ugandan general who lobs grenades on Twitter 
  - Published30 October 2022
In his posts, Gen Kainerugaba accused the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR), an armed group operating in eastern DR Congo, of targeting members of the Bahema ethnic community.
The Bahema are a traditionally cattle-herding community mainly based in DR Congo's north-eastern Ituri province.
They have historical and cultural ties to the Bahima people of neighbouring Uganda.
He also threatened a rebel takeover of Walikale, in North Kivu province, while defending Uganda's military presence in DR Congo.
Walikale is rich in mineral resources , including some of the country's largest tin deposits and several major gold mines.
Gen Kainerugaba's X account, which had nearly 1.4 million followers, has since become inaccessible.
It is unclear whether he deactivated it, as he has done in the past, or whether the platform had suspended it.
During the same week he declared: "My tweets in Uganda are directives that must be obeyed."
The posts followed reports that a DR Congo military aircraft had allegedly been shot down by rebels, with foreign mercenaries reportedly among those on board.
Gen Kainerugaba criticised the reported presence of foreign mercenaries in DR Congo.
"These remarks, which are particularly serious, have caused a major media incident and undermine the necessary restraint that must prevail in relations between sovereign states," the DR Congo foreign ministry said in a statement on Wednesday.
"The Congolese government expects the Republic of Uganda to clarify its official position and take the necessary measures to prevent such transgressions from recurring in the future".
The ministry added that DR Congo remained committed to regional peace and stability but would defend its dignity and institutions against "any form of provocation or interference".
It is not the first time Gen Kainerugaba's social media posts have strained relations between the two countries.
In February last year, he threatened to seize the eastern DR Congo city of Bunia, claiming that members of the Bahima ethnic community were being attacked.
In 2024, DR Congo also summoned Uganda's diplomatic representative after the general made threats against foreign mercenaries operating in eastern DR Congo.
The 52-year-old general, widely seen as a potential successor to his father Yoweri Museveni, has become known for his provocative social media posts.
In 2022, he sparked a diplomatic row with neighbouring Kenya after threatening to invade the country and capture its capital, Nairobi, prompting his father to apologise forn the remarks.

items.text:
17. Lions' Commentary on Unix
Lions' Commentary on Unix
John Lions was teaching operating systems at the University of New South Wales in Australia.
What's the best way to
teach operating systems?
They need to study the Unix source.
But it's tough going.
I'll write my
own textbook.
In May 1976, Lions prepared lecture notes explaining the kernel source code of AT&T's Unix Version 6. These became his Unix commentary.
To understand an OS,
we need to read
the actual code.
I've written a guide
to the Unix kernel.
We'll use it as
our textbook.
By 1977, the notes were circulating among other schools and research institutions with Unix licenses [1][4]. Even Bell Labs wanted copies and eventually took over distribution [2].
Early on, Unix source could be studied in class. But at USENIX in June 1979, AT&T announced new Version 7 license terms restricting courses that disclosed or discussed source code. Distribution of Lions' book was tightly controlled as well [5][6].
I am altering the license.
Pray I don't alter it
any further.
Destroy Lions' book.
No more teaching
Unix source code.
There is no escape
from our operating system.
He's teaching from the Unix source code!
Seize the books!
Run!
He's got the book!
Don't let him
escape!
Quick! Take
the book!
Ugh!
I find your interest
in source code disturbing.
Just use the system calls.
Learn a little theory.
Leave the internals to us.
Theory isn't enough.
I need to see the code.
This code is our only hope
of understanding an OS.
For roughly twenty years before the official edition appeared, computer-science students studied from unauthorized photocopies. The book helped a generation of students learn to build operating systems of their own [5][8].
Meanwhile, members of the Unix community, including Peter H. Salus, Dennis Ritchie and Berny Goodheart, kept asking AT&T, Novell and the Santa Cruz Operation for permission to publish the book. SCO finally agreed. Peer-to-Peer Communications published the official edition in 1996 [5][7].
Lions' book is finally
in print. It even has
my foreword.
People were secretly copying it
for twenty years?
Unbelievable.
You can read a reconstructed version of the commentary as a PDF, or order a print copy on Amazon. The Unix Version 6 source code is available separately from TUHS.
References
- Lions' Commentary on UNIX 6th Edition, with Source Code
- John Lions, Lions' Commentary on UNIX 6th Edition, with Source Code, Peer-to-Peer Communications, 1996 (ISBN 1-57398-013-7).
- System call
- UNIX News, Vol. 2 No. 3, March 1977 - John Lions's March 11, 1977 letter and the announcement of book distribution to Unix licensees.
- Rachel Chalmers, "Code critic", Salon, November 30, 1999 - recollections from students and Dennis Ritchie, distribution restrictions, and the path to publication.
- Peter H. Salus, The Daemon, the GNU and the Penguin, Chapter 6: "1979", 2005 - the Version 7 license terms announced at USENIX in June 1979 and restrictions on classroom use.
- Dennis Ritchie's October 22, 1995 letter and Peter H. Salus's July 12, 1996 letter - publication-permission correspondence preserved by Warren Toomey.
- MIT, "Xv6, a simple Unix-like teaching operating system", "History and Background" - teaching with Lions's commentary and the background to xv6.

items.text:
minipg is PostgreSQL as one executable, ready to use, with no server to configure. A .pgdb directory is the database: its data, config, credentials, and Postgres version all live inside it, and minipg app.pgdb opens a psql shell on it. A server starts when a command needs one and stops on its own when it's idle.
minipg embeds Docker Hub's postgres:18-alpine image and runs it with h9, used as a Zig library. h9's Linux personality runs Alpine's own Postgres binaries directly on the host's hypervisor, with h9's Plan 9 kernel answering their system calls. There's no Linux kernel to boot, no VM image, and no Docker.
The demo downloads about 35 MB. It needs JavaScript Promise Integration, which Chrome and Edge have from version 137; other browsers are getting it. It can also be opened on its own page.
The demo runs minipg's Linux build, which runs inside the Postgres image itself. It starts Postgres as ordinary processes and serves on a unix socket, since a page has no TCP. New databases come from a template cluster made at build time, because initdb takes half a minute on v86.
minipg app.pgdb                     # psql shell (creates app.pgdb if missing)
minipg app.pgdb "select 1"          # one statement
minipg url app.pgdb                 # postgres://postgres:...@127.0.0.1:54321/app
minipg serve app.pgdb               # an explicit foreground server
minipg run app.pgdb -- npm start    # your app, with DATABASE_URL set
minipg dump app.pgdb > dump.sql     # and minipg restore app.pgdb dump.sql
A .pgdb holds minipg.toml (settings and the generated superuser password) and pgdata/, Postgres's data directory as plain files. A stopped one can be copied like any directory. New clusters use Postgres's builtin C.UTF-8 locale, which sorts the same on every platform.
In CI, the Linux binary is static and needs no privileges or devices: without /dev/kvm, h9 runs Postgres on its native backend. A test job can be as small as:
minipg init test.pgdb
minipg run test.pgdb -- go test ./...
The README lists every command, and the manual is the full guide.
Exactly one process runs Postgres for a .pgdb, enforced by a lock. It holds the server's h9 machine, whose Linux root is the unpacked image and whose writable working directory is the .pgdb. The image's docker-entrypoint.sh initializes the cluster on first start. Commands never host Postgres themselves. If no server is running, they start one in the background and use it. psql, pg_dump, and the other tools each run in their own short-lived h9 machine (about 90 ms to start) over the same root.
The source is on GitHub, under the MIT license. Building needs Zig 0.16, plus curl, jq, tar, and xz for the root:
git clone --recursive https://github.com/progrium/minipg
cd minipg
make build         # pulls the root for this host's arch, builds ./minipg
make root ARCH=386
make web           # this page's demo, in .zig-out/web
minipg is early, and h9's Linux personality is young. On h9's native backend, Postgres is about 2x slower than native for one client, and slower under load. Don't trust it with data you can't recreate yet.
Please report bugs and send questions through GitHub issues.

items.text:
As foreign troops withdraw from Somalia, could al-Shabab take over?
- Published
Somalia is facing a fresh test of its stability as foreign troops begin withdrawing, funding for its security forces comes under pressure and a bitter political dispute threatens to derail plans for the country's first direct democratic elections in decades.
The combination of challenges has raised questions about whether the government can defend itself against Islamist militant group al-Shabab while managing growing divisions among political factions.
Some analysts fear the situation could embolden al-Shabab, which is affiliated with al-Qaeda, and potentially allow it to seize control of the capital, Mogadishu.
The group already controls large parts of the country despite the presence of about 12,000 African Union (AU) troops supporting the government.
The withdrawal of foreign forces, alongside the activities of clan-based militias aligned with rival political factions, has heightened concerns about the government's ability to maintain control.
Ugandan troops, who make up the largest contingent of the AU force, began withdrawing last month, with the country expected to complete its withdrawal by next year.
Ethiopia, another major contributor to the AU mission, is also reportedly planning to withdraw about 3,000 troops. The country has 2,500 troops authorised under the AU mission and roughly 5,000 under a bilateral agreement with Somalia. It is not clear whether the reported withdrawals would be from the AU contingent, the bilateral force, or both.
The US, which had earlier announced cuts to funding for the UN Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS) has since said it is extending it for a year. Washington contributes about a quarter of $500m UNSOS's annual budget, which supports Somali security forces, AU missions and individual troop-contributing nations.
With military support uncertain and the government facing mounting political challenges, analysts question whether Somalia's security forces are ready to stand on their own.
The concerns were heightened recently when al-Shabab claimed to have killed hundreds of elite Somali soldiers in an attack. The government acknowledged the attack but did not disclose the number of casualties.
Abdisalam Guleid, a former deputy director of Somalia's National Security Agency, told the BBC the security situation was increasingly precarious.
He warned that the withdrawal of foreign troops could leave Mogadishu vulnerable to a takeover similar to that of Afghanistan by the Taliban in 2021, following the withdrawal of US and Nato forces.
"I don't think Mogadishu will be able to defend itself. The Taliban style [takeover]… that's the most likely scenario I can envision now," he said.
The Taliban took over control of Afghanistan between 6-15 August 2021 in a rapid offensive, following the withdrawal of US and NATO forces.
Such a scenario has played out in Somalia in the past, Guleid explains.
- Why is Uganda fighting in 'hellish' Somalia? 
  - Published15 March 2012
Somalia has experienced the collapse of central authority before.
In the early 1990s, clan-based rebel groups advanced on Mogadishu from several fronts, forcing then-President Mohamed Siad Barre from power.
His overthrow triggered a devastating civil war and a prolonged humanitarian crisis. The collapse of state institutions subsequently created conditions in which Islamist militant groups, including al-Shabab, were able to expand their influence.
Guleid says Ugandan troops have been central to preventing a similar collapse since their first deployment to Somalia in 2007.
They played a key role in driving al-Shabab out of Mogadishu and other major towns, while protecting strategic installations, including the airport, seaport, government institutions and diplomatic missions.
Troops from Burundi, Djibouti, Kenya, Sierra Leone and Ethiopia later joined the AU mission, while countries including Turkey and the US maintained separate military deployments and provided training and equipment to Somali forces.
But Guleid argues that years of international assistance have not translated into sufficient military independence for the Somali government.
He says the authorities have become so reliant on foreign protection that they have neglected to adequately prepare their own forces to take over.
Somalia's Information Minister Abdifatah Qasim Mohamud rejected suggestions that the country would be unable to cope with the withdrawals.
He told the BBC that Somali troops had already taken over some positions vacated by Ugandan forces and were prepared to assume greater responsibility for the country's security.
He said Somalia could not depend indefinitely on foreign troops for its protection.
"I believe there is no reason for concern over this issue. There will be no change in the country's security situation or in the areas they have vacated," he said.
President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud has also been seeking continued international backing.
During a visit to Uganda on 23 November, he and President Yoweri Museveni called on the international community to continue supporting Somalia to consolidate security gains.
Not everyone believes the withdrawal will necessarily result in a security collapse.
Ugandan security analyst Freddie David Egesa argues that years of international military support have helped Somalia establish the institutions needed to take greater responsibility for its security.
He says the withdrawal will provide an opportunity to assess how much progress has been made.
It will also force Somalia's political leaders to put aside their differences and take greater responsibility for the country's future, he adds.
But other analysts warn that the timing could hardly be worse.
Omar Mahmood, an analyst at the International Crisis Group, says Somali forces are under considerable pressure as they fight al-Shabab while attempting to take over positions previously held by foreign troops.

Ask HN: Why is Ask HN only showing me 14 posts? - https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49984484 - Oct 2026 (47 comments)
Ask HN: Why is pagination gone on "Ask HN", and showing only 19 items? - https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50280719 - Oct 2026 (3 comments)
I believe I found the problem. The pool of stories for https://news.ycombinator.com/ask has traditionally been drawn from the ranked stories list from which we generate the frontpage. That list is restricted to the top 1500 ranked submissions, and it seems the % of submissions which are text posts (i.e. no linked URL) had declined enough to starve the Ask HN feed. The solution is to compute a separate list of ranked Ask HNs.
p.s. "Ask HN" is the conventional name but it means text posts. The title can also start with "Tell HN" or nothing in particular. They're just posts which were submitted without a URL.

items.title: Has global jihadism failed, or is it simply changing shape?
items.summary: Rice, pasta, sugar, cooking oil and beans are hardly what you'd expect to see in jihadist propaganda. Yet these were among the supplies that al-Qaeda's Somali branch, al-Shabab, said its "charity" had handed out to hundreds of struggling families in August, as it publicised the aid through its socia
items.text:
Rice, pasta, sugar, cooking oil and beans are hardly what you'd expect to see in jihadist propaganda. Yet these were among the supplies that al-Qaeda's Somali branch, al-Shabab, said its "charity" had handed out to hundreds of struggling families in August, as it publicised the aid through its social media accounts and radio station.
The group, which controls large parts of rural southern and central Somalia, has been keen to show off its so-called humanitarian work throughout 2026.
"May God reward them," said a local woman in one of al-Shabab's videos.
It's all part of an effort to win over local communities and present itself as more than just a jihadist group.
A quarter of a century after al-Qaeda's 9/11 attacks in the US, and 12 years after Islamic State group (IS) declared its so-called caliphate in Iraq and Syria, the jihadist movement looks very different.
Rather than focusing on attacking the West or fighting for a global Islamic state, some - especially those linked to al-Qaeda - are putting more effort into winning power closer to home. And they seem increasingly willing to make compromises along the way.
Because of this, a debate is growing within the movement. While hardliners reject compromise, pragmatists see working with local groups and former enemies as a way to gain power. But do the pragmatists represent a genuine change or simply a shift in tactics to achieve the same ultimate goals: establishing a state that applies their strict interpretation of Islamic Sharia law both at home and in its dealings with the outside world?
Significant defeats
Neither al-Qaeda nor IS has achieved its ultimate dream: taking over one or more countries and ruling them according to their strict interpretation of Islam.
Both have suffered major defeats, lost leaders and faced years of international pressure. IS, which once controlled vast areas of Iraq and Syria, lost its last territorial stronghold in 2019. But jihadism hasn't gone away.
Africa is now the main battleground for jihadism, with al-Qaeda's powerful branches, JNIM in the Sahel (Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger) and al-Shabab in Somalia, fighting long-running insurgencies. IS, its bitter rival, has active branches in Nigeria, the Democratic Republic of Congo, the Sahel, Mozambique and Somalia.
One major source of inspiration, and envy, whether jihadists admit it or not, is Syria's new president, Ahmed al-Sharaa. The former IS and then al-Qaeda commander was once wanted by the US but rose to power in Syria in December 2024 and was welcomed by Western leaders.
Once known by his militant nom de guerre Abu Mohammed al-Jolani, he led the jihadist group Nusra Front - initially linked to IS and then al-Qaeda - and later the group Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS).
He gradually broke ties with both IS and al-Qaeda and distanced himself from their calls for global jihad.
Instead, he focused on Syria, building a local power base in the north-western Idlib province.
What surprised everyone was his growing willingness to work with non-Islamist groups and engage with foreign powers. As HTS advanced on Damascus, its leadership sought to reassure the international community, reaching out even to Russia, a key ally of then-president Bashar al-Assad, to allay fears of an Islamist takeover.
That pragmatism, combined with favourable geopolitical conditions - including a weaker Russia and Iran - helped him take power in Syria.
But the sight of him being welcomed by world leaders, including US President Donald Trump, was even more remarkable.
During Sharaa's visit to the White House in November 2025, Trump sprayed him with his own branded cologne, jokingly asked how many wives he had and praised him as a "very strong leader".
For some jihadists, Sharaa's success has been inspiring. Others, however, see his actions as a betrayal of everything they believe in.
IS has declared jihad against Syria's new Islamist government, branding Sharaa and his officials "apostates", and has carried out attacks against government forces on that basis. Other hardline clerics have taken a similar stance, but have stopped short of openly calling for jihad against Sharaa.
The divide between hardline jihadists and their more pragmatic counterparts has fuelled a bitter online debate since 2025, with rival voices trading accusations of betrayal and even publishing competing books to defend their positions.
For hardliners, going too far can mean abandoning their core beliefs. This might include holding back from imposing their strict version of Islamic law, accepting "man-made" laws or a constitution, taking part in elections, working with non-Islamist groups, or building ties with governments they consider "infidel".
Another source of inspiration for jihadists was the Taliban's return to power in Afghanistan in 2021, as it showed that an Islamist movement could eventually take control of a country after years of fighting Western-backed forces. It engaged local groups, slowly secured power across the country, used international diplomacy, and bided its time before taking the capital, Kabul, in a lightning offensive.
A means to an end?
Two groups are especially worth watching: al-Qaeda's branches in Mali and Somalia.
In late April, al-Qaeda's Sahel branch, known as JNIM, showed considerable pragmatism by joining forces with nationalist Tuareg separatists - whom it had occasionally fought - to launch a major offensive that threatened Mali's military rulers. It even went as far as to call the Tuaregs "brothers".
But it's not just JNIM's growing military strength that's attracting attention. It's also how the group is presenting itself.
Its propaganda once prominently featured al-Qaeda's leaders, slogans and calls for global jihad. Since late 2024, however, its videos have dropped the familiar al-Qaeda branding.
And instead of talking about global Muslim causes, JNIM has increasingly focused on local problems, portraying itself as a defender of ordinary people against corrupt and abusive ru

Hospitals nearby treated patients suffering burns and
items.text:
At least 30 killed in massive fire as fuel tanker crashes on Cairo highway
- Published
At least 30 people have been killed and 19 others injured in a large fire on a busy highway in Cairo after a fuel tanker crashed, Egypt's health ministry says.
Hospitals nearby treated patients suffering burns and smoke inhalation after the incident, which occurred on a section of a ring road in the Warraq neighbourhood, to the north of the old city centre, on Wednesday evening.
Unverified footage circulating on social media showed billowing flames and black smoke towering high into the night sky, with multiple nearby vehicles torched.
Officials have not given an account of how the fire broke out, but state-owned media reported the tanker had overturned, dousing nearby vehicles with petrol.
The regional public prosecutor has launched an investigation into the incident and asked that DNA samples be taken from bodies of the dead.
The tanker, which belonged to a private contractor, had been travelling along the highway when a high-voltage cable fell in front of it, prompting the driver to lose control, Al-Ahram reports, citing sources with knowledge of the investigation.
It then crossed the central reservation, overturned and caught fire, the state-owned newspaper says.
Egypt has suffered several deadly fires in recent years, with informal residential areas and often run-down infrastructure making incidents more common, the response to which is often complicated by slow emergency response times and locally improvised rescue efforts, even in the sprawling Egyptian capital.
Images from the scene show a large crowd gathered on the highway after the fire had been extinguished, as emergency services blocked off entry routes.
The health ministry said 39 ambulances had been dispatched to respond to the fire, while it posted images of Egypt's health minister overseeing the treatment of the injured at one of Cairo's hospitals.
Road collisions are also common in Egypt, often attributed to lax maintenance and the widespread flouting of traffic laws.
Nearly 6,000 people died on Egypt's roads last year, official figures show, a rise of several hundred on the previous year's total.
Emergency responders have since cleared the highway and allowed it to reopen, state broadcaster NMA reports.
A bulldozer could earlier be seen at the scene clearing the burnt-out wrecks of cars.

items.text:
'Justice for sport' - reaction to Afcon final verdict
- Published
"Justice for sport."
That was the initial reaction of Senegal football federation (FSF) president Abdoulaye Fall to the decision by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) to reinstate the West Africans as 2025 Africa Cup of Nations champions.
The Teranga Lions beat Morocco 1-0 in January's final but were stripped of the title in March by a Confederation of African Football (Caf) appeals board, which imposed a 3-0 forfeit after they walked off the pitch in protest at a penalty awarded against them when the game was goalless.
Following a hearing in Lausanne in October, a three-man Cas panel unanimously overturned that ruling by Caf, effectively judging that the decisions taken by referee Jean-Jacques Ndala in restarting the match and playing it to a conclusion were final.
Morocco's football federation (FRMF), however, says it will "pursue all available legal avenues to challenge the decision".
The North Africans could yet take their fight to the Swiss Federal Court.
Those in Senegal have celebrated the return of the title, while several legal experts have backed the Cas verdict.
- Senegal reinstated as Afcon 2025 winners by court ruling 
  - Published1 day ago
Teranga Lions pay tribute to fans
Senegal's talisman Sadio Mane, who was named player of the tournament at Afcon 2025, said the ruling "fills us with joy".
The 34-year-old former Liverpool man thanked his team-mates and Senegal staff as well as the whole Senegalese nation at home and abroad.
"Your faith in us gave us strength during the most difficult moments. This victory is yours, too," he said in a statement on social media.
Senegal captain Kalidou Koulibaly, who missed the final through injury, echoed that sentiment.
"Some victories are won on the pitch, while others are won in the heart of a people," he said in a post on Facebook.
"This one is both.
"Long before this verdict, there was you - your prayers, your flags in the windows, your fervour, and the pride that unites us all: the pride of the people of Teranga."
Pape Gueye, the man who scored the extra-time winner in Rabat, described the Cas decision as "an immense relief".
Both he and Mane had a message of support for Morocco.
"Senegal and Morocco are brotherly nations; may our shared passion for football continue to bring us closer together," Mane said.
Gueye added: "Beyond football, the respect and fraternity between our two peoples remain what matters most. Let's hold on to that.
"In the end, it is Africa that wins."
Moroccan dissent continues
Morocco's main complaint is that Articles 82 and 84 of Afcon tournament regulations - which were implemented by the Caf appeals board in March - were not followed by Cas.
Article 82 states that if a team "refuses to play or leaves the ground before the regular end of the match without the authorisation of the referee" it shall be "considered [the loser] and shall be eliminated for good from the current competition".
Article 84 then states a 3-0 forfeit should be imposed on a team which is eliminated in such circumstances.
"There [are] football rules that should have been applied by the referee," former Morocco international Hassan Kachloul told BBC Sport.
"When the Senegalese players left the pitch, the game should have been over."
The FRMF registered its "surprise" at the Cas decision and said that the panel "failed to account for the stance recently established" by the International Football Association Board (Ifab), the game's ultimate lawmakers, and world governing body Fifa regarding players leaving the field of play without the referee's permission.
However, Ifab only updated its laws in April - three months after the Afcon final - to state that a referee may send off any player who leaves the field when protesting a decision.
Moroccan football journalist Jalal Bounouar says his compatriots are "frustrated and disappointed" by the ruling.
"The main reason is that Caf's appeal board had already applied Article 82 and 84 of the competition regulations which considered Senegal to have forfeited the match," he told Newsday on the BBC World Service.
"Many Moroccans feel the decision by Cas has ignored the importance of these rules. From the Moroccan perspective, the referee should have taken stronger disciplinary action.
"We feel that our team was put in a difficult situation and that the final was not managed fairly."
The legal verdict
Cas has a long-standing practice of following what has been called the 'field of play' doctrine.
It refrains from "reviewing decisions taken on the playing field by referees for applying the rules of the game, unless there is evidence that those rules were applied arbitrarily or in bad faith".
"The primary argument was that the referee is the master of the decision on the pitch," said Serge Vittoz, a member of the FSF's legal team.
Raymond Hack, both a former head of disciplinary at Caf and a former arbiter at Cas, said the judgement was the "correct verdict".
"What everyone seems to forget - and whilst there may be contradictory information in Article 82 and 84 - decisions taken by the referee during the match are final," the South African told the BBC World Service.
"That's the end of the story.
"Only the referee can start a game. Only a referee can end a game."
For former Nigeria striker Daniel Amokachi, an Afcon winner in 1994, the Cas ruling is "the right decision".
"At the end of the day, the man in charge of the match (Ndala) restarted the game, the game ended," he said.
"He has a final say."
The questions for African football
Caf has already tightened its own regulations to avoid a repeat.
But Algerian sports journalist Maher Mezahi says the continental governing body still needs to salvage its image.
"How many times have we seen Caf's legal institutions, whether it be the disciplinary board or the appeals committee, come up with these decisions that we all find ridiculous," he said.

items.summary:
Five Mexicans arrested in Nigeria over $227m meth lab
- Published
Five Mexican nationals and a Nigerian businessman have been arrested in Nigeria after authorities uncovered an industrial-scale methamphetamine laboratory, the country's drug enforcement agency says.
More than 1.5 tonnes of the highly
items.text:
Five Mexicans arrested in Nigeria over $227m meth lab
- Published
Five Mexican nationals and a Nigerian businessman have been arrested in Nigeria after authorities uncovered an industrial-scale methamphetamine laboratory, the country's drug enforcement agency says.
More than 1.5 tonnes of the highly addictive synthetic drug, commonly known as meth, was seized from the facility in the south-eastern state of Enugu. The haul included both finished drugs and meth still being produced.
The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) estimates the drugs are worth $2267m (£1723m).
It is the fourth industrial-scale meth laboratory with alleged links to Mexican drug cartels to have been discovered in Nigeria in recent months.
The Nigerian businessman, 63-year-old Chuks Enoch Ezeike, also known as "Over Size", is accused of setting up the laboratory and smuggling the five Mexicans into the country using forged Argentine, Colombian and Chilean passports.
The NDLEA identified the five as Oscar Ramos-Cardenas, who it described as the alleged leader of the group, Juan Antonio Sarabia-Cabrera, Luis Enrique Garcia-Amador, Jose Alejandro Renteria-Reyes and Salomon Cabanillas-Torres.
The laboratory, situated behind an oil company in Enugu, also had accommodation for the Mexican nationals, allowing them to live and work there without attracting attention, the agency said.
Speaking at a news conference in the capital, Abuja, on Wednesday, NDLEA chief Mohamed Buba Marwa said the arrests followed a seven-month investigation involving several countries.
The agency had been monitoring Ezeike since April, when it received intelligence allegedly linking him to Ramos-Cardenas, a Mexican national suspected of specialising in large-scale meth production.
In August, the five Mexicans were refused entry into Nigeria after arriving at Abuja's international airport and were sent back to Mexico.
But less than a month later, they tried again, travelling through Colombia and France before arriving in neighbouring Benin, where they were allegedly given forged passports.
This time, Nigerian authorities deliberately allowed them into the country, Marwa said.
"We wanted the whole network: the meth specialist, the financier, the factory and the product. Sending them home a second time would only have postponed the problem," he said.
The men were allegedly met by Ezeike in Lagos before being taken to Enugu, where they were kept under surveillance.
More than 200 anti-narcotics officers were deployed on 11 November to raid the laboratory and a hotel where Ezeike was staying in simultaneous operations.
The five Mexicans were arrested while producing the drug, the agency said. Ezeike told investigators they had been due to leave Nigeria two days later.
Nearly seven tonnes of chemicals used to manufacture meth, as well as industrial equipment, were also seized.
The NDLEA said Ezeike had admitted owning the laboratory and bringing the Mexican nationals into Nigeria to produce the drug.
Investigators believe the operation was part of a wider international criminal network in which a Mexican cartel recruited and paid specialists to manufacture meth, while Nigerian collaborators allegedly provided the facilities and resources.
The agency has not identified the Mexican cartel it suspects was involved or said whether the six suspects have been formally charged.
The arrests come amid growing concerns about Mexican drug cartels setting up production bases in West Africa, a region long used as a transit route for illicit drugs.
While some of the meth produced in the region supplies a growing local market, traffickers also target lucrative overseas markets, particularly in Europe and Asia.
Earlier this year, Nigerian authorities uncovered similar laboratories in Ogun, Oyo and Ebonyi states.
The latest operation brings to 10 the number of suspected Mexican meth production specialists arrested in Nigeria in recent months, according to the NDLEA. Five others arrested in earlier operations are already in custody awaiting trial.
Issuing a warning to foreign drug cartels, Marwa said: "Nigeria is not your laboratory. It is not your warehouse, and it is not your transit route."

- Published
A Zimbabwean court has issued an arrest warrant for Bellarmine Chatunga Mugabe, the youngest son of the country's late former president Robert Mugabe, after he failed to appear in court.
Mugabe was arrested ear
items.text:
Zimbabwe issues arrest warrant for Robert Mugabe's son over missed court date
- Published
A Zimbabwean court has issued an arrest warrant for Bellarmine Chatunga Mugabe, the youngest son of the country's late former president Robert Mugabe, after he failed to appear in court.
Mugabe was arrested earlier this month alongside four others over assault allegations on a police officer during an investigation into the suspected smuggling of luxury vehicles.
The group subsequently faced charges of robbery and malicious damage to property. They have yet to enter pleas.
They were granted bail on 6 November and were due back in court on Tuesday. However, Mugabe failed to attend. His co-accused, an aide and three security guards appeared and were remanded until 10 December.
Prosecutors allege that Mugabe and the others assaulted an investigating officer using their hands and broomsticks.
The officer's phone was allegedly taken and smashed on the ground, while one of the accused is said to have seized the officer's loaded pistol.
Bellarmine Chatunga is the youngest son of Robert Mugabe and his second wife, Grace Mugabe.
Robert Mugabe ruled Zimbabwe for 37 years before being forced from power in 2017, aged 93, following a military intervention. He died in 2019.
His son has attracted public attention in recent years over a series of legal troubles and his high-profile lifestyle.
Last month, he admitted to drug-related charges involving the possession of cannabis.
In April, he was deported from neighbouring South Africa after pleading guilty to pointing a firearm and being in the country illegally. He had been arrested following the shooting of a 23-year-old man at his home.
In 2023, he was arrested in Harare, Zimbabwe's capital, over allegations that he damaged property and spat at a police officer during a party.
He was later freed after reaching an out-of-court settlement with the complainant, who was a friend.

- Published
A South African court is due to rule on President Cyril Ramaphosa's attempt to overturn a report that found he has a case to answer over the theft of large sums of cash from his private farm.
In 2022, an indepe
items.text:
Court to rule on South African president's bid to set aside 'Farmgate' report
- Published
A South African court is due to rule on President Cyril Ramaphosa's attempt to overturn a report that found he has a case to answer over the theft of large sums of cash from his private farm.
In 2022, an independent panel said Ramaphosa may have committed serious misconduct relating to the theft of $580,000 (£443,000), hidden in a sofa, at his Phala Phala game farm in the Limpopo province. He denied any wrongdoing.
Ramaphosa challenged the findings of the report after the Constitutional Court ruled that parliament had violated the constitution by blocking moves to impeach him.
The ruling could either exonerate the president or clear the way for him to possibly face impeachment.
Wednesday's ruling will be handed down by the Western Cape high court - the same court that blocked a parliamentary committee from proceeding with the impeachment process while a review challenge of the report is under way.
The scandal, dubbed "Farmgate" by local media, has has dogged Ramaphosa since it emerged in 2022, when former spy chief Arthur Fraser reported the matter to police in a dossier.
Fraser, an ally of former President Jacob Zuma, accused Ramaphosa of concealing the theft from the police and tax authorities.
The break-in happened in 2020, when thieves allegedly stole bundles of US dollar bills hidden inside a sofa at the farm.
Earlier this month, two people were found guilty of the theft.
Ramaphosa confirmed that a robbery had taken place but said the money had been from the legitimate sale of buffalo from his livestock business.
Several investigations cleared him of any wrongdoing, but parliament began an impeachment proceedings in 2022 and appointed an independent panel to investigate the allegations.
The panel made a series of damaging findings, including that there was "substantial doubt about the legitimacy of the source of the currency that was stolen".
It also concluded that Ramaphosa "has a case to answer".
Ramaphosa initially challenged the report in court but withdrew his application after parliament voted against adopting its findings.
He revived the legal challenge again in May this year after the Constitutional Court, the country's highest court, ruled that parliament had acted unconstitutionally by blocking moves to impeach him.
It ordered parliament to refer the report to an impeachment committee.
In his latest challenge, Ramaphosa argued that the panel had "misconceived its mandate, misjudged the information placed before it and misinterpreted the four charges advanced against me".
If the Western Cape High Court rules in his favour, it could bring the current impeachment process to an end, unless parliament successfully challenges the decision.
A ruling against him would allow the parliamentary committee to examine the charges against the president and make a recommendation.
If the committee recommends impeachment, parliament would have to vote on whether to remove him from office. This would require the support of at least two-thirds majority in parliament.
Ramaphosa's Africa National Congress (ANC) has enough parliamentary seats to block such a move.
He is the first president to face impeachment proceedings under the rules introduced in 2018.
